It should be understood that in all such cases, the former [faults] are grave while the latter is light.
Fourth, praising oneself so as to cause others to imitate and practice [such faults] also varies in degree among individuals,
and thus the resulting harm is either light or heavy.
Furthermore, it can be known that there are cases where one’s own roots of goodness are exhausted to form grave offenses.
Fifth, regarding the mind, there are four types.
First, if, for the sake of causing others to give rise to faith, one praises oneself and disparages others.
1. This is merit and not an offense.
2. If one commits an offense through a negligent or neutral state of mind, it is an offense but not defiled.
3. If one commits an offense out of attachment or aversion toward another person.
These are defiled but not grave.
Fourth, those committed out of greed for fame, profit, offerings,
and honor are grave but not light.
This fourth [category] has three grades. First,
if it arises from the manifestation of afflictions that are not extremely intense, or if one feels shame and remorse,
this is the inferior grade.
Although these two may at times be intense, they lack shame and dread of blame;
they have not yet been seen to function as virtues,
and thus they still belong to the medium grade.
If one lacks shame and remorse, develops deep attachment and delight, and views the act as a virtue,
this is called the highest grade, the most grave. Furthermore, within this category,
an offense committed with a mind of greed and delusion is considered grave.
Other states of mind may be light or involve no offense;
other meanings should be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Sixth, regarding the practitioner:
Within the Buddha-dharma, practitioners generally initiate their practice according to four categories:
namely, the three trainings and miscellaneous practices.
First, regarding the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*), there are two types.
First, feigning eccentricity:
this refers to those who, though they do not violate the precepts, are by nature not upright;
relying on false deliberations, they manifest an appearance of extraordinary deportment.
They dazzle the world in pursuit of fame and profit;
they lack a fundamentally pure mind for seeking liberation.
Yet, they universally disparage others who possess no different outward demeanor, claiming them all to be devoid of virtue.
These are thieves in the guise of śramaṇas, and they are also thieves of dignified deportment (īryāpatha).
This is as taught in the Kāśyapa-sūtra, the Ratnakūṭa-sūtra, and other such texts.
Second, regarding those of shallow understanding:
This refers to those whose nature lacks profound wisdom,
who rely on their own observance of precepts as the means for liberation,
and who look down upon others who are diligent in the Vehicle but lax in their observance of precepts.
To hear that all phenomena are empty and immediately give rise to fear—
this is an enemy and thief of the Buddha-dharma.
(From the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra*).
Second, regarding those who study by convention, there are also two types.
The first concerns those who are greedy and deceptive;
that is, those whose nature delights in fame and profit, yet have long resided in the mountains.
With their minds slightly clarified and tranquil, they manifest signs of meditative concentration;
dazzling the world, they attract great fame and renown,
while universally disparaging others who lack such signs as being incorrect.
"This is an araṇya-thief. This is from the *Puṣpahasta-sūtra*.
Furthermore, another sūtra says:
Wearing patched robes in secluded places and calling themselves *araṇya-dwellers*, etc.
Second, regarding those who possess false pride:
this refers to those whose nature is not one of great learning, yet who rely on mountains to practice meditative concentration.
When spirits and deities cause one's mind to become fixed in concentration,
and one perceives the unwholesome thoughts of others,
one immediately waits for this to arise and conceives pride.
They will then attract great fame and reputation, looking down upon and despising others while regarding all their views as wrong; they will harm the Buddha-Dharma.
These are the great thieves of Māra.
According to the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* and the *Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
there are also two categories regarding those who train in wisdom (*prajñā*).
The first concerns those of shallow capacity.
This refers to those who, by nature possessing little intelligence, lack systematicity in their recitation and study;
yet, driven by a mind agitated by fame and profit, they rush forward to preach prematurely,
making arbitrary judgments based on their own views to disparage both the ancients and the present.
Seeking only fame and profit, they originally have no intention of renunciation;
relying on their own lack of practice, they also hold the precepts and meditative concentration in contempt.
These are thieves who sell the Buddha-dharma.
This will bring about great suffering.
This is from the section on the deeds of Māra within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Second, regarding the profound [meaning]:
This refers to those whose nature is characterized by limited discernment;
although they have a slight understanding of the words and meanings of the Tripitaka of the Two Vehicles,
they have still not grasped the Buddha’s intent.
Now that you have been entrusted with the transmission of the Dharma, you should instead praise merit and virtue to encourage future students;
rather than disparaging the ancients and the present, you should aspire to stand alone in excellence.
Yet, relying on this as a virtue, you give rise to arrogance and treat others with contempt.
If one merely recites and maintains the medicinal Dharma yet fails to extinguish the illness, one has already incurred the fault of defilement;
how much more so when one further gives rise to illness within the Dharma—this is truly beyond salvation!
Alas, how could fire produced from water ever be extinguished?
These are thieves who destroy the Buddha-dharma.
From the *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha-sūtra*:
"Fourth, regarding those of mixed conduct, there are also two types."
First, regarding those who practice for the sake of merit:
their nature is not upright, but rather they are devious and crafty,
collectively pursuing extraordinary meritorious acts to dazzle the world and attract generous offerings.
The intention is to call out for many by means of a few,
using this as a livelihood.
Once their desire is fulfilled, they rely upon this and give rise to conceit.
They despise others who lack gain and offerings,
regarding them all as being improper;
such is their attitude toward gain and offerings.
The same applies to those who seek fame;
these are thieves who sell the Buddha-dharma.
This is from the Kāśyapa Sūtra.
Second, concerning other practitioners:
this refers to those whose nature is not awakened by wisdom;
as soon as they study a single teaching, they become attached to it and are deluded by what they have studied, seeking thereby to attract fame and profit.
To dismiss all other practices as not being ultimate is likewise a foolish person who harms the Buddha-dharma like a pestilence;
this concludes the brief enumeration of the four positions above.
In truth, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are permeated by deception and falsehood;
they should all be examined accordingly.
I exhort all later students not to allow their own minds to fall into this trap.
One should immediately read and take to heart such scriptures as the *Ratnakūṭa*, the *Ratnāvalī*, and the *Kāśyapa-parivarta*.
Only by thus nurturing the bodhicitta can one consider it essential.
Seventh, there are three ways in which one obtains the fruit of retribution.
First, regarding the general discussion,
the *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"Bodhisattvas have four kinds of ways that lead to downfall."
First, lacking respect for others;
second, ingratitude and sycophancy;
third, seeking excessive gain, offerings, and fame.
Fourth is feigning goodness and proclaiming one's own virtues.
These are the four dharmas that lead to downfall.
Second, specifically regarding the disparagement of others:
As stated in the *Sūtra on Slandering the Buddha*,
there were ten people who slandered the Dharma Master Eka-pratibhāna-śikṣita,
whereby the Buddha-dharma in that region declined to some extent.
These ten people later fell into hell, where they endured sufferings such as having their tongues torn out for immeasurable kalpas.
Subsequently, they were born many times without eyes.
Finally, they encountered Śākyamuni Buddha.
Having gone forth for a long time and completed ascetic practices without attaining anything, he subsequently fell back again;
this is explained at length.
Thirdly, there is a specific section on self-praise.
For example, there were five people such as Śaṇḍila;
four sat in the forest while one went into the village and proclaimed:
In a forest there was an arhat who received great offerings;
later, he fell into hell and underwent all manner of sufferings,
and after emerging from it, he became a human being.
He acts as a porter for his original donors, a bearer of their sedan chairs, or a carrier of their refuse vessels, and so forth,
as detailed extensively in the Vinaya texts. Eighth,
regarding the practitioner who maintains and repairs [the dwelling], there are three meanings.
A bodhisattva constantly reveals his own faults so that others may hear and know them;
he does not harbor even a single thought of concealment,
fearing that they might increase and worrying that they would be difficult to extinguish.
One should never proclaim one's own virtues,
nor give rise to even a single thought of self-glorification;
for fear of depletion and concern that they will not increase.
Second, Bodhisattvas should always perceive only the good and not the evil in other sentient beings. Therefore,
they endure the evil directed at themselves and attribute goodness to others,
so that their minds remain constantly pure.
This is their constant practice.
Question: If one recognizes what is not evil as one's own and pushes aside what is good in others, is this not indeed sycophancy and false speech?
Answer: Since one dwells in a state of insufficiency, how could one be without fault?
It is said that only the Buddha alone is without fault.
Because all defilements have been exhausted;
furthermore, that other goodness which remains without remainder is itself the Buddha-nature,
which is true goodness.
If the mind reaches this point and recognizes the investigation,
it is not merely free from flattery nor free from false speech;
rather, it gives rise to immeasurable roots of goodness.
One maintains the precepts for the sake of purifying them.
Third, a bodhisattva should never dwell in places where fame arises or where material gain is abundant,
because such things cause harm.
The Treatise says:
"Gain and offerings are like frost and hail,
for they damage the sprouts of merit."
Furthermore, just as with a rope made of hair,
because it is so harmful,
one must avoid it from afar even if it has been obtained in accordance with the Dharma.
The Sūtra states:
"When offerings and gain arrive, one should avoid them by traveling three *yojanas* away;
how much more so those obtained through praise or disparagement that are contrary to the Dharma?"
Therefore, it is logically improper for a bodhisattva to engage in such actions.
The *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"There are four kinds of dharmas that should be abandoned."
First, the bodhisattva abandons the household life;
second, having gone forth, they do not crave gain and offerings;
third, they distance themselves from all donors.
Fourth, not sparing one's own body or life.
These are the four dharmas that should be relinquished.
The same principle applies here.
Within the ninth section on the universal and the specific, there are two parts:
first the universal, then the specific.
Regarding "eloquence," there are three types.
First, to clarify "self-praise," there are likewise three:
first, praising the Dharma one practices oneself so that others may cultivate and study it.
Second, to cause those sentient beings who have not yet developed faith to do so;
third, to increase the faith of those who already possess it.
If there is truly such benefit, and one does not harbor greed or pride nor engage in self-praise, there is no offense.
One does not praise that which is faulty because it is contrary to benefit.
Second, the explanation of disparaging others also has three parts:
first, disparaging false paths to cause them to return to right view.
Second, one censures those who cling to wrong views to cause them to abandon their attachment;
third, one censures those who engage in evil conduct to cause them to desist from it.
If one does not mix this with anger or pride, and if it is timely and beneficial, there is no offense in censuring others.
Not disparaging those who have committed offenses.
Regarding the three types of seeking fame and profit, there are two [categories]:
first, for the benefit of sentient beings.
Second, because one seeks the true fame and profit that transcend the world,
this seeking is not an offense;
it is not sinful to seek them.
It should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the two restricted cases:

within the three aforementioned categories, whether collectively or individually, one gives rise to a thought of desire to commit an offense through a mind associated with the *paryavasthāna* (envelopments).
Although it may not yet constitute a grave offense, it is nonetheless a transgression;
because it harms the Dharma, one must guard against it with great care.
The remaining meanings can be understood accordingly.
Tenth, regarding the explanation of the text:
within the first section, which raises faults and establishes the formal regulation, there are two parts;
first, raising the faults, which also consists of two parts.
Regarding the stage of the first offense:
as with one's own actions and instructing others, there should likewise be four [categories],
though they are omitted here for brevity as in the previous case.
Second, the characteristics of the offense.
Fourth, the offenses are the same as before;
they are also identical to the three explanations.
The self-praise is omitted;
logically, it should possess four [aspects].
First, with respect to the capable agent.
First, greed, pride, and so forth serve as the causes;
second, fame, profit, and the like serve as the conditions;
third, the skillful establishment of rules and models that constitute the method for self-exaltation and the disparagement of others serves as the dharma.
Fourth, constantly making this [behavior] one's habitual activity.
Second, regarding the object [of the action]:
first, instead of praising or censuring correctly, one merely speaks of their causes, thereby causing one's own virtues to be proclaimed.
Because others are disparaged, it is called the "cause";
because one's own lineage and so forth are disparaged, it is called the "condition.
The same applies to self-praise.
Third, because one disparages the Dharma upon which others rely and so forth, it is called "Dharma.
Fourth, because one disparages the karma upon which others rely and so forth, it is called "karma.
The same applies to self-praise.
Regarding the threefold synthesis:
first, the internal cause;
second, the external object.
Third, adding disparagement;
fourth, completing the karma.
Self-praise is also like this.
The preceding section concludes the enumeration of faults.
According to the above, there should be a second text here concerning the formal regulation, which should state:
"In all cases, one must not praise oneself or disparage others."
Furthermore, it is also a brief summary of what was not fully detailed.
Thirdly, from "the bodhisattva" onwards, the text clarifies that which should be practiced;
this also explains the reasons for establishing the regulations mentioned above.
This refers to the fact that the Buddha specifically prohibited praising oneself and disparaging others.
Since it is in accordance with the Dharma for Bodhisattvas to take upon themselves the abuse and injury intended for others,
failing to do so would contradict the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
How much more so when one further adds self-deprecation;
because such opposition and harm to the settled sincerity are profound, a grave offense is established.
This is the meaning of the text.
Within this context, unreasonable oppression and deception are termed "inflicting injury," while causing another to feel shame and seek retribution is termed "humiliation.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) for the sake of sentient beings.
He resolutely causes sentient beings to abandon their evil tendencies until they are completely exhausted.
Therefore, the evil deeds of sentient beings are the responsibility of the bodhisattva,
because he has taken them upon himself through his commitment to gathering them in.
Because one has already cultivated roots of goodness for the sake of sentient beings,
and because one's own roots of goodness are shared with others,
they must be bestowed upon them.
The fourth [section]: if one exalts oneself and disparages others, it constitutes an irrational transgression; this may be understood accordingly.

8. The Eighth Chapter: On the Precept Against Avarice. Regarding the original intent of this initial regulation:
First, because giving (*dāna*) is the foremost of the ten thousand practices,
and because it encompasses the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*),
it constitutes the relinquishing of stinginess to accomplish generosity.
Briefly stated, there are ten points,
as set forth in the "Chapter on the Ten Practices" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding the first practice,
Joyful Conduct: this bodhisattva acts as a great donor.
They are able to relinquish all that they possess;
they bestow gifts upon all sentient beings with an impartial mind,
and having given, they feel no regret.
They do not hope for karmic retribution;
they do not seek fame or reputation;
they do not seek birth in superior realms.
Not seeking gain or offerings.
As for the ten [qualities]:
first, desiring solely to rescue and protect all sentient beings.
Second, the desire to gather in all sentient beings;
third, the desire to benefit all sentient beings;
fourth, the desire to study the original practices of all Buddhas.
First, the desire to correctly focus the mind on the original practices of all Buddhas;
second, the desire for the purification of the original practices of all Buddhas;
third, the desire to receive and uphold the original practices of all Buddhas.
Eighth, wishing to manifest the original practices of all Buddhas;
ninth, wishing to extensively expound the original practices of all Buddhas;
tenth, wishing to cause all sentient beings to leave suffering behind and attain the bliss of nirvana.
These are the ten.
From this, one should know that there is no practice of giving that is not within the principle of a bodhisattva.
Second, regarding the explanation of the name:
To be stingy with wealth and the Dharma, failing to provide for those who seek them, is called "habitual avarice" (*mātsarya*);
the precept against stealing is established as its antidote,
and its name is derived based on this primary condition.
Regarding the three stages:
first, one praises oneself and disparages others in order to seek fame and profit;
second, one wastes time in the pursuit of wealth not yet obtained.

Now, regarding the stinginess of one who has already acquired wealth for oneself and refuses to relinquish it; while the former [type of stinginess] pertains to the time of accumulation, this refers to the time when that period has passed.
The former is coarse, whereas this is subtle.
It comes here because of the sequence of its meaning.
Regarding the fourth point, the completion of the offense through the presence of conditions:
within this precept, there are four points at which an offense is committed.
First, stinginess oneself;
second, teaching others [to be stingy];
third, rejoicing [in such stinginess].
Fourth is the praise of stinginess.
For now, let us briefly distinguish its conditions based on oneself;
the remaining three [types of stinginess] may be inferred accordingly.
It is accomplished through the presence of six conditions:
first, possessing one's own wealth and Dharma;
second, the presence of a petitioner.
Third, possessing both of the two aforementioned perceptions;
fourth, giving rise to a mind of stinginess and malice;
fifth, being directly opposed to the object-condition.
Sixth, because the preceding person is empty and turns back.
Fifth, regarding the deficiency in the meaning of conditions:
first, there are three meanings concerning the deficiency of the initial condition.
First, if there is not even a single needle or blade of grass that can be given away,
one should console and thank the beggar with kind words, a profound mind, and falling tears,
while simultaneously forming this thought:
"I am now of little merit and cannot fulfill the aspirations of sentient beings;
this is my own fault.
I shall practice with diligent effort so that these vows may be fully realized"—thus he spoke, and acted with such diligent vigor.
This is called non-offense.
Second, if one relies on the pride of having no possessions and fails to apologize without feeling shame or regret,
one should incur a minor offense (duṣkṛta).
Third, if one is a beggar and the donor does not believe that one has nothing, yet repeatedly suppresses and presses for more,
such that one gives rise to a mind of resentment, one commits an offense of intermediate gravity.
If one immediately gives rise to anger, one commits the subsequent precept against anger.
The same applies to the gift of Dharma.
Next, regarding the omission of the second condition, there are four meanings.
First, there is no offense if no one asks.
Second, regarding one's own wealth and so forth:
if one sees a person suffering from greed who is either unable to beg or too ashamed to beg,
yet does not give, this also constitutes an offense.
Third is the wealth of one's own possessions.
Seeing fellow practitioners who lack food and clothing and thus neglect their correct practice,
that person restrains themselves and neither seeks [resources for them] nor gives [what they have], thereby committing an offense.
Fourth, one first stores up much wealth;
although there are no beggars, one does not give as an offering to the field of merit.
Thus, these latter three cases all incur the offense of failing in skillful means.
Because it does not constitute a direct commission of a grave offense, there are two absences of the third condition.
First, this refers to the fact that in each of the two aforementioned stages, there are two distinctions: perception and doubt.
If one perceives that there has been no offense, or if one suspects that there was an offense through preparatory effort,
both cases may be judged accordingly.
There are two cases for the omission of the fourth condition:
if one does not grant [the request] because one is subduing the other with a mind of compassion, there is no offense;
if it is done with a neutral (avyākṛta) mind, the offense of preparatory action (prayoga-āpatti) may be understood to apply.
Next, the fifth omission has four points:
first, whether one grants or does not grant [the precepts], one commits a grave offense;
second, if one grants them, it is only a minor offense.
Third, granting the superior while withholding the inferior;
fourth, giving later when the time has passed.
The latter three all involve skillful means.
Next, the sixth omission has two aspects:
first, if it is not empty [of the intention] and one does not turn back, there is no offense;
second, if although it is empty, the intention has not yet been severed despite the lack of turning back, there is an offense of preliminary effort (prayoga).
Sixth, regarding the gravity [of offenses], there are five factors:
first, in terms of the object;
second, in terms of the field [of merit].
Third, in terms of impairment;
fourth, in terms of the mind;
fifth, the combined explanation.
At the beginning and middle [of this teaching], there are the gifts of wealth, Dharma, and fearlessness. There are three types of the gift of wealth:
namely, external, internal, and both.
Regarding external material wealth, ten types are generally enumerated:
first, food and so forth;
second, medicine and so forth.
1. The three robes and so forth;
2. the four requisites and so forth;
3. domestic animals and so forth.
Sixth, slaves and servants;
seventh, fame and reputation;
eighth, royal status.
Ninth, wives and concubines;
tenth, sons and daughters.
In all these cases, each preceding category does not overlap with the subsequent ones.
One should not subsequently treat [the person] with contempt.
Second, within the internal body, there are five [aspects]:
first, temporarily requesting their service.
Second, seizing the hair, nails, and so forth;
third, intending to make them slaves;
fourth, seizing their limbs, joints, and blood in its entirety.
Fifth, taking the body and life in their entirety.
Among these, each preceding offense is more grave than the one following it,
while each succeeding offense is less grave than the one preceding it.
Of the two types of Dharma-giving, there are three:
first, worldly dharmas;
second, the dharmas of the Two Vehicles.
There are three dharmas of the bodhisattva path;
likewise, there are three types of fearless giving.
The first is the relinquishing of evil.
Second, abandoning suffering;
third, saving life.
In the first two cases, the gravity of the offense is lighter if the preceding conditions were not fulfilled.
It should be understood that each subsequent category does not carry as much weight as the preceding one.
Second, regarding the field (*kṣetra*), there are four types.
First is the field of gratitude (*upakāra-kṣetra*), which refers to parents, teachers, masters, and so forth.
Second is the field of virtue, referring to the Three Jewels and so forth.
Third is the field of compassion, referring to sentient beings who are hungry and destitute and so forth.
Fourth is the field of suffering, referring to sentient beings who are in distress and adversity and so forth.
In all cases, that which precedes does not constitute a grave offense;
that which follows should be considered light.
Third, regarding those who cause harm:
Regarding each of the four aforementioned objects, there are two types:
first, causing their lives to end by failing to provide them with sustenance;
second, causing them great suffering and the like, even though their lives do not come to an end.
In all cases, it can be understood that the preceding is heavy and the succeeding is light.
Regarding the fourth point, concerning the mind, there are likewise the three poisons—whether single, paired, or combined—and so forth;
these should be understood by analogy with what was stated above.
Furthermore, stinginess has three grades.
That of the householder Luṭi and others is the heaviest;
the medium and lower grades may be understood accordingly.
Fifth, regarding the analysis by way of combination:
either when one gives rise to superior stinginess toward inferior objects in relation to a superior object, it is most heavy;
or when one gives rise to inferior stinginess toward superior objects in relation to an inferior object, it should be light.
The remaining phrases are to be understood accordingly.
Regarding the seventh, those who receive retribution, ten types are briefly distinguished:
first, being born among the hungry ghosts.
As in the case of Maudgalyāyana’s mother and others;
secondly, those who suffer in other realms of existence,
such as the scabies-afflicted jackal.
3) Even to the point that there is not a single hair with which one can cover the body;
4) one undergoes the suffering of poverty and destitution among human beings;
and 5) one's roots of merit from previous lives are exhausted and diminished.
Fifth, one fails in the bodhisattva’s perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Sixth, due to stinginess regarding the Dharma, one constantly suffers from ignorance throughout successive lifetimes.
The *Susheng jing* (Sūtra on the Birth of Goodness) says:
If there are those who give rise to stinginess regarding material wealth, the Dharma, or food,
one should know that such persons will receive the retribution of deluded poverty for immeasurable lifetimes.
Furthermore, because they conceal the Dharma-eye, they shall forever remain without eyesight.
Eighth, because they do not bestow fearlessness, they will always harbor terror throughout their lives, never finding even momentary peace.
Ninth, enemies will constantly find opportunities to exploit them.
Tenth, it causes the three types of giving and the six perfections to fail to be accomplished.
The remainder is as explained elsewhere.
Regarding the eighth practice of remediation, ten types are briefly presented.
First, one contemplates that both one’s own body and material possessions are impermanent phenomena subject to decay and extinction.
Once they have fallen into ruin, there is no way to preserve them even with regret;
therefore, stinginess and attachment are of no benefit whatsoever.
Furthermore, both are shared by kings, thieves, water, fire, wicked sons, and others.
Since it has not yet been stolen, one should quickly relinquish it as a gift and place it in a secure storehouse so that it remains one's own forever.
Third, if one is stingy and does not give, one plants the karma for poverty in life after life, which follows along with oneself.
Fourth, because I did not habituate myself to giving in previous lives, I now possess wealth yet am stingy and unable to give.
If I do not now exert effort in giving,
this habit will not be broken but will further increase, thereby obstructing great generosity.
I should now exert my resolve to overcome stinginess and practice generosity.
Furthermore, if one is personally impoverished and fears being unable to survive,
yet remains stingy and does not give, one should reflect as follows:
Poverty is an obstacle to giving.
To overcome this obstacle,
one should endure hardship and exert effort in practicing generosity.
"Due to my past karma, I have previously endured various sufferings such as hunger and thirst,
yet I was unable to benefit even a single sentient being.
Now, by practicing generosity, I am able to benefit others."
Even if it meant undergoing manifold sufferings until the end of their lives, they would never allow a beggar to return empty-handed;
how much more so when there are still remaining vegetable leaves and such that can sustain life?
Therefore, one should endure this poverty and suffering and practice giving.
Sixth, if one is unable to relinquish one's body, life, or cherished wealth, one should reflect as follows:
"When I previously gave rise to the great bodhicitta before the Great Teacher of the triple world,
I had already relinquished all things, both internal and external.
How could I now violate my original vow and betray sentient beings?"
Seventh, if I were to cause myself to commit a *pārājika* offense against the bodhisattva precepts,
I would be deceiving the Buddhas of the ten directions;
this is utterly unacceptable.
"8. Now I renounce this non-solid, foul-smelling, and impure body.
Now I shall attain the pure Dharma-body, which is the solid dharma.
This will truly benefit me."
If one does not practice giving, one will lose great benefit.
Ninth, this body and these riches are illusory things;
yet, one should not fail to relinquish them to fulfill the wishes of sentient beings.
"How can I possibly benefit sentient beings with unsurpassed bodhi?
Tenth, I should contemplate that all phenomena are empty and devoid of self or what belongs to a self;
yet now, regarding this false body and wealth, I am stingy and unwilling to relinquish them."
How can one realize and enter into the nature of equality?
By contemplating these ten kinds of remedies,
there is nothing among all forms of stinginess that one cannot relinquish.
This is fully as explained in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
and other texts. Regarding the ninth point, the distinction between universal and specific, it is based on the thirty-ninth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Briefly, there are thirty types of non-giving that do not constitute an offense.
First, if one knows that various internal or external objects of giving would bring only pleasure, but no benefit, to those sentient beings; or if they would bring neither pleasure nor benefit.
In both cases, he does not give anything away.
Second, if there are those who come seeking him as a companion with the intent to act unrighteously— by means of coercion, injury, or deception toward others.
Consequently, one does not give even one's own body to them.
Third, if a bodhisattva’s intention for practicing generosity is pure,
and they see immeasurable matters for benefiting sentient beings directly present before them.
Even if someone should come seeking one's own limbs and joints,
one should not give them away.
Fourth, if the hosts of Māra harbor a mind of affliction and disturbance.
If someone appears and requests one's own body, limbs, or members,
one should not grant them; for by doing so,
one would incur a grave transgression and, contrary to one's intention, cause harm to that person.
Fifth, there may be sentient beings who are deluded, crazed,
or mentally deranged and come to request the limbs and members of the Bodhisattva’s body;
these should not be given.
Sixth, if there are sentient beings who, whether for their own harm or for the harm of others,
come seeking such things as poison, fire, weapons, or intoxicants,
one should not give them these items.
Seventh, one does not practice giving by using another's property as if it were one's own.
Eighth, one does not practice giving by acting as a matchmaker for marriage or by giving away the wives or concubines of others.
Ninth, one does not practice giving with food, drink, or other items that contain living organisms.
Tenth, if there are sentient beings who come seeking various things that incite frivolous pleasure or lead to what is meaningless,
one should not give them;
for this would cause them to frequently engage in arrogance, negligence, and unwholesome conduct.
After the dissolution of the body, they will fall into the various evil destinies.
Eleventh, one must never provide others with items for hunting and the like.
Twelfth, there may be sentient beings who are about to be killed.
He never gives them away.
Thirteenth, if there are those who come seeking nets, traps, or snares for the purpose of harming sentient beings or for the sake of practice and study, [he does not give them].
In all such cases, they do not give anything away.
Fourteenth: if an enemy comes seeking vengeance, desiring to revile, bind, imprison, kill, plunder their wealth, or inflict punishment upon them.
He never gives them away.
To state it briefly:
he does not give away any instruments of play or pleasure that oppress or harm sentient beings.
Fifteenth, if there are those who come seeking food and drink that is immoderate or unsuitable,
one likewise does not give it to them.
Sixteenth, if there are sentient beings who, having already eaten their fill, are by nature excessively gluttonous.
They repeatedly come to seek rare and exquisite food and drink,
yet he does not bestow any upon them.
Seventeenth, if there are those who come to seek their parents, teachers, or elders...
He certainly does not give them away.
Furthermore, regarding his own wives, children, slaves, servants, and kinsmen,
if he does not first instruct them with correct speech to make them joyful, [he does not give them away].
19. He never compels those who come seeking gifts to feel distress or anxiety;
rather, he first uses correct speech to instruct and persuade them, causing them to rejoice and develop a mind of joyful aspiration.
20. Furthermore, one does not bestow [remedies] upon enemies, evil friends, or rākṣasas who wield weapons;
nor does one bestow them upon those beings who are intensely afflicted and who delight in practicing various kinds of violent and evil deeds.
One must never grant the royal throne to those who come to seek it.
Even if such an evil person already occupies the throne,
a bodhisattva who possesses the power should still depose them.
How much more so when it comes to giving them away?

Twenty-first: furthermore, bodhisattvas never seize or plunder the wealth and possessions belonging to their parents, wives, children, slaves, servants, messengers, or kinsmen and relatives in order to use them for the purpose of giving.
Twenty-second, he does not distress his parents, wife, children, slaves, servants, or kinsmen and relatives by giving away the objects intended for them to those who come seeking alms.
Twenty-third, he does not do so through unrighteous means or with violence.
Furthermore, they do not practice giving by coercing or harming others.
Twenty-fourth, if bodhisattvas have gone forth within the holy teachings of the Buddhas,
they never transgress any of the training rules while practicing giving.
Twenty-fifth: Furthermore, bodhisattvas never bestow upon those who come seeking things that are inappropriate for them;
that is to say, they do not give leftover food or overnight meals to those who have left the household life.
Or it may be mixed or defiled by various excretions, mucus, saliva, vomit, pus, blood, or other impurities;
furthermore, it may not have been announced so that [the recipient] is unaware of it, such as food discarded according to the rules or the meat of a deer.
That is to say, giving to those who do not eat onions food mixed with onions or tainted by onions;
giving to those who do not eat meat food mixed with meat or tainted by meat;
and giving to those who do not drink alcohol food mixed with alcohol or tainted by alcohol.
26. Furthermore, bodhisattvas never orally transmit any of the true Dharma to non-Buddhists who seek out faults; 27.
nor do they bestow upon them the scriptures they have transcribed.
Twenty-eighth: if one knows that the person has a nature of excessive greed and seeks to trade or sell scriptures and the like, one shall not bestow them upon them.
Twenty-ninth: if one knows that the person desires secret treasuries, one shall likewise not bestow them upon them.
In the thirtieth [case], one does not seek superior wisdom nor bestow it upon others.
Furthermore, regarding those who do not give as described above,
the Bodhisattva cannot bear to say directly, "I will not give to you."
One must skillfully instruct and exhort them to perform a "purifying gift" (śuddhi-dāna) by first relinquishing all their personal wealth,
provisions, and belongings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
Just as a bhikṣu performs the ritual of pure giving (*śuddhadāna*),
when observing a supplicant and bestowing a gift,
he should properly form this thought:
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have no small thing whatsoever that they do not bestow upon sentient beings.
Having understood this, one takes things and gives them away;
yet, if at the time of giving one observes that it does not accord with the correct principle, [one should not give].
One should immediately recall the previously performed rite of pure giving (śuddhaka-dāna) and declare:
"This object belongs to another."
Unable to grant it to you,
he used gentle words of persuasion and skillful means to send you away.
Furthermore, in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*:
Even if a newly initiated bodhisattva has someone come to request their head, eyes,
or other limbs, yet is unable to give them away,
they should speak this verse:
When I first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment,
my roots of goodness were not yet matured;
may I swiftly achieve fulfillment.
Later, we must certainly examine the treatises together.
Regarding the two restricted cases:
one should simply observe oneself; as soon as even a slight afflictive thought arises, one should immediately give.
Otherwise, one commits an offense.
If it concerns the secret [teaching],
a bodhisattva should be extremely stingy.
This refers to begging for the life-preserving raft of the precepts without yielding even a speck of dust,
and harboring great fear even toward minor transgressions, and so forth.
The tenth section, the explanation of the text, also consists of four parts.
First, clarifying the status of the offense:
this refers to committing it oneself or instructing another to do so, as explained previously.
Second, within the section on citing faults and establishing the formal prohibition, there are two parts.
First, the faults are raised.
That is to say, regarding the dharma and karma caused by stinginess, there are also four explanations,
which may be understood as being the same as before.
Second, from "When the Bodhisattva has seen [this]" onwards, it clarifies the formal regulation.
This refers to the regulation for giving to the poor and beggars.
However, among worldly people, there are two kinds of poverty.
First, poverty of material wealth;
second, poverty of the Dharma.
Hence it is said that they are "poor in every respect."
Because a bodhisattva gives these two things, it is said that "everything is bestowed.
Thirdly, a bodhisattva commits an offense by acting contrary to the established rules through an evil disposition;
this refers to one who possesses an evil mind.
The fetter of stinginess is not severed;
it is also a transgression of non-giving that extends to other afflictions.
Regarding "a mind of anger":
it refers to being enraged at a beggar and failing to give.
This explains the lack of generosity; below, the objects that are not given are clarified.
"Material wealth first, then the Dharma," and so forth,
up to "not practicing giving," etc., are cited as examples where minor matters are mentioned while major ones are omitted.
One would not give even a single leaf of grass,
let alone many;
furthermore, since this is stated with reference to the lowest possible limit, it says "even down to a single blade of grass," and so forth.
"One speck of dust within the Dharma" means that it is intended to clarify what is extremely small;
it does not mean that there are actual atoms within the Dharma-gates.
This follows the linguistic conventions of the Western regions (India),
as seen in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, where it says,
"there is not even the slightest dharma."
In the Sanskrit original, it is titled "The Dharma Without Even a Single Atom.
That one should instead revile and insult [this teaching] reveals an extremely grave state of mind;
to cherish even a blade of grass while giving rise to intense anger [toward the Dharma] is a sign of such severity.
Because one utters evil words and gives rise to insults and humiliation, the offense is appropriately grave.
This can be understood as encompassing the three types of karma.
Fourth, the conclusion indicating the name of the offense can be understood.
9. Therefore, regarding the precept against anger, the first section of the nine precepts against anger: the original intent for its initial formulation was briefly based on ten reasons.
First, because among all afflictions, none is more grave than this.
Second, because these two also constitute the paths of unwholesome action that lead to the miserable realms;
third, because they incinerate all roots of goodness from previous lives;
and fourth, because they can bind one in great enmity that remains difficult to resolve for many eons.
Fifth, because it is capable of harming sentient beings;
sixth, because it can even lead to the commission of an *ānantarya* (immediate) offense;
and seventh, because it can obstruct the bodhisattva’s perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Eighth, because it harms the great compassionate mind of all bodhisattvas;
ninth, because it causes those beings to be converted to abandon [the path];
tenth, because it fully accomplishes hundreds of thousands of obstacles.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* quotes extensively,
stating further:
"I do not see a single evil dharma that surpasses a bodhisattva’s single thought of anger."
Since the harm is already so extreme, it must be restrained.
Second, as for the explanation of the name:
it refers to the arising of a mind of harm toward an adverse object.
Because the precepts prevent these faults, they are given this name.
Regarding the third sequence:
it follows because greed and attachment are followed by anger.
The fourth, the possession of conditions, consists of two factors:
first, an opposing object that possesses resistance;
second, the arising of the perception thereof.
Third, not restraining the mind;
fourth, committing an offense as soon as anger arises.
These are categorized according to the mind.
If one extends this to both body and speech and further subjects the other to beating and abuse,
the offense is incurred through five conditions.
If one takes it to the extreme and, even when the other person comes to apologize, one’s anger remains unresolved, [the offense is complete].
One commits an offense through six conditions.
Regarding the deficiency of the fifth condition,
there are three ways in which the first condition may be deficient.
That is to say: the characteristic of sentient beings,
the characteristic of non-sentient things,
and the characteristic of both sentient and non-sentient things.
If the mental expectation or both [the intention and the object] are grave,
while the physical or verbal act itself is light;
next, there are also three cases where the second condition is missing.
This refers to fundamental delusion, perverted perception, and doubt;
these are to be understood as grave when associated with the mind,
while they may be light when manifest through body and speech.
There are two deficiencies regarding the third condition:
first, constantly and diligently cultivating the light means for remedying lost mindfulness;
second, failing to diligently cultivate the heavy means [for remedying it].
Next, the fourth condition is absent in three cases:
namely, when there are low, middling, or superior [degrees of anger]. If one gives rise to a low degree of anger and immediately feels regret, the preparatory effort is light.
Second, if one gives rise to a low degree of anger and does not feel regret, the preparatory effort is heavy.
Among the three types of arousal, if anger arises and one immediately generates remorse, it constitutes a heavy preparatory effort (*prayoga*);
the others may be understood as entering the category of heaviness.
This is when viewed in relation to body and speech.
Omission, striking, and verbal abuse are grave when the preparatory means are heavy;
conversely, they are light. To speak in terms of the ultimate limit: [the gravity of the offense depends on these factors].
Furthermore, there is the method of generating a sense of heavy remorse through further repentance;
conversely, failing to do so constitutes a heavy offense.
Sixth, regarding the gravity of offenses:
Briefly summarized, they are distinguished according to five positions:
first, according to the object;
second, according to causal matters.
Third, according to the characteristics of the afflictions;
fourth, according to their formation and impairment;
fifth, a combined analysis.
Briefly, there are ten types of objects toward which anger arises at the beginning and middle [of its development]: first, noble beings;
second, teachers.
Third, one's parents;
fourth, those who transmit the Dharma;
fifth, the Saṃgha.
Sixth, laypeople;
seventh, one's own disciples, both male and female;
eighth, servants and slaves.
Ninth, animals;
tenth, insentient objects.
In comparison with the precepts, both are grave.
In terms of the paths of action, one expects that the former are heavy and the latter are light.
Second, regarding the causes and matters:
briefly, anger arises from ten matters as its causes.
First, it contradicts one's own views and understanding;
second, it contradicts one's own desires and inclinations;
third, it encroaches upon one's own fame and profit.
Fourth, the loss of one's own kinsmen;
fifth, being reviled for no cause;
sixth, being unjustly beaten and bound.
Seventh, dismembering his limbs with a sword;
eighth, about to take his life;
ninth, harming his parents.
Tenth, destroying the Triple Gem.
Because of these ten matters, anger arises;
in all cases, the preceding is more serious than the succeeding.
Third, regarding the characteristics of the afflictions, ten types are also distinguished:
first, the face becomes flushed with anger as soon as it arises, without any change in complexion;
second, the complexion changes in the opposite manner.
Third, the entire body trembles and quivers;
fourth, one additionally strikes and reviles;
fifth, regarding what has arisen above, one immediately repents as soon as it arises.
Sixth, one repents only after six nights have passed.
Seventh, one does not relinquish it for a long time.
Eighth, when the other person briefly apologizes, one immediately resolves the offense.
In nine cases, people seek repentance for a long time before they are released;
in ten cases, they seek repentance for a long time yet are not released.
It can be understood that in all instances, the offense was light at first and became heavy later.
Fourth, regarding those who cause harm, ten types are also briefly manifested:
first, out of anger toward others, causing them to abandon the Buddha-dharma;
second, further uttering evil abuse.
Third, striking with a staff and binding;
fourth, damaging another's property;
fifth, severing another's limbs and joints.
Sixth, to sever the life-root of another;
seventh, to harm one's own relatives;
eighth, to permanently abandon the Triple Gem.
Ninth, burning monasteries and harming monks;
tenth, committing various heinous crimes.
In all these cases, the offenses become progressively more grave.
The fifth combination also reveals ten stages;
that is to say, among the aforementioned four, it is the most grave when one gives rise to intense anger toward a venerable object for a minor cause and inflicts great harm.
The remaining cases correspond respectively; furthermore,
there are varying degrees of lightness and heaviness for those that do not correspond,
which can be understood by reflecting upon them accordingly.
Regarding the seventh point, the attainment of retribution, ten types are briefly shown.
First, through anger one incurs ten offenses, as described in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on Knowledge).
Second, due to hatred, one enters the eight great hells,
as stated in the first fascicle of the *Śīlasūtra*.
Third, one also falls among the hungry ghosts and animals.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
"Among the offenses of anger and hatred, the most severe are the cause for rebirth in hell;
those of middling severity lead to rebirth as an animal."
The lower [state] is that of the hungry ghosts (preta).
The above are the fruits of retribution (vipākaphala).
As for the four fruits of uniform outflow (niṣyandaphala):
The Sūtra says:
"If one is born among humans, one receives two kinds of retribution:
first, one is constantly sought out by others for their faults."
Second, one is constantly afflicted and harmed by others.
Regarding the five types of dominant results (*adhipati-phala*) in terms of the external environment (*niśraya-vipāka*),
the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, chapter seven, states that due to hatred (*dveṣa*), the flavor of the fruit becomes bitter and pungent.
Sixth, one's physical form is perpetually ugly, such that people take no pleasure in seeing it.
Seventh, one loses the meditative bliss of the higher realms.
Eighth, one deviates from the liberation of the two vehicles.
One should understand that there are nine harms to the bodhisattva’s two types of beneficial conduct and ten losses regarding the bodhisattva’s five stages.
The eighth [section], on the practice of cultivation:
a brief exposition on contemplating ten kinds of antidotes to prevent anger from arising.
First, contemplation.
All sentient beings, from time immemorial,
have never failed to be my parents, relatives, kinsmen, preceptors, or elders. Therefore,
one should simply give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and filial piety toward them.
How could one possibly harbor anger and resort to beating or reviling?
Second, contemplate impermanence.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Whether born or growing, each and every one of those sentient beings is subject to the law of impermanence and death.
The ultimate repayment of enmity is said to be the severing of their lives;
yet the lives of these beings are severed moment by moment.
For what reason would a wise person wish to further sever that which exists among sentient beings as this impermanent phenomenon of birth and death?
A wise person should not give rise to a defiled mind of attachment toward such existence.
How much more so when one is subjected to harm by hand, clods of earth, or staffs;
how much more so when one's life is entirely cut short.
Therefore, one is able to endure all such enmities and injuries.
Third, the contemplation of suffering.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"Furthermore, all bodies, whether one's own or those of others, have the nature of suffering as their essence."
Because they lack knowledge, they further increase their suffering upon the inherently painful nature of my body.
Since I possess knowledge,
why would I further add suffering to that inherently painful nature for them?
Furthermore, even those sentient beings who possess great prosperity are constantly pursued by the three types of suffering;
how much more so those who are in decline?
I must now apply diligent skillful means to cause them to be free from all suffering.
One should not inflict further suffering upon them.
Fourth is reflection on the conditions of karma:
"I am currently without fault, yet they have unjustly subjected me to beating and abuse."
This must be due to past causes and karma; for if it were not so,
how could there be the retribution of suffering arising without a cause?
Since it is established that [suffering] is one's own karma,
one should not feel anger toward others.
As a verse in the *Saṃbhāra-śāstra* says:
Whether beaten, reviled, threatened with death, or bound,
one should never harbor resentment or blame others;
all this is my own fault.
They appear due to the ripening of karma;
five types of volitions increase suffering.
That is to say, because I previously afflicted others with suffering and harm, I have now invited this suffering and affliction upon myself.
If I were now to be unable to endure it, I would further plant the causes and conditions for great suffering in the future.
If I do not abandon these causes of suffering,
I am bringing about what is unwholesome for myself.
Thus, one creates for oneself the bonds of affliction and gives rise to enmity and harm by oneself;
it does not come from another.
Sixth, regarding compassion for the foolish:
in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*,
it is stated that if one strikes or reviles a person who is intoxicated by alcohol or possessed by a ghost, [there is no offense].
Thus, one does not become angry with them.
Sentient beings are likewise:
intoxicated by the wine of ignorance and possessed by the demons of affliction, they are driven about and lack self-mastery.
Therefore, one should not become angry;
rather, one should simply think:
"This fault belongs to the afflictions, not to the blame of sentient beings."
I shall diligently seek enlightenment in order to treat the disease of afflictions for all sentient beings, ensuring they are forever cured.
Seventh, he further reflects:
"If I do not take birth in a pure land, a place free from affliction..."
Since one has already been born in this defiled land,
it is natural that one should undergo affliction;
however, one should instead subdue one's own mind in order to seek liberation.
One should not become angry with them.
Just as when entering a thicket of thorns, it is the nature of things that one will be pricked; one should simply seek to escape and not become angry with the thorns.
Eighth, furthermore, through reflection:
"I have myself generated the bodhicitta to bear the heavy burden for the sake of all sentient beings;
even if it were the suffering of hell, I would undergo it for their sake."
How much less can I endure this minor suffering and thus violate my original vow?
If I cannot endure it, I am not self-subdued;
how then could I cause others to abandon their afflictions?
Therefore, one should not become angry.
Ninth, one further reflects:
"I am now training in the practices of all bodhisattvas."
Among the practices of a bodhisattva, the practice of patience is supreme;
neither the observance of precepts nor ascetic austerities can equal it.
This practice is fundamentally perfected only through the presence of harm and provocation.
If there were no such affliction, my practice would not be perfected;
that person has bestowed a great practice upon me,
and I should therefore feel shame and offer thanks.
If one does not express remorse and apologize, one also incurs a profound transgression.
How can you turn your back on such kindness and instead respond with anger and vexation?
This is utterly improper.
As the Sūtra says:
"Devadatta is a great spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
This is precisely what that refers to.
Tenth, one further contemplates the absence of intrinsic nature in causes.
As the Sūtra says:
"It is by means of the hand, the sword, the staff, and the body of the self that striking is accomplished."
"I should not now direct my anger toward another out of malice.
The commentary explains:
"Because he has committed the act of striking, one who feels anger toward him [is acting improperly]."
Furthermore, since it is because of me that you strike,
why do you not direct your anger toward yourself?
Moreover, since striking arises from conditions, it must lack intrinsic nature.
Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are ultimately empty.
Since both the striker and the struck are non-existent,
even patience cannot be established.
How can one become angry?
The *Dharmapada* says:
"Know that anger and the like are like a mirage."
Patience is also that which has nothing to endure.
As a verse in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-saṃyukta-śāstra* says:
"The body, enemies, swords, and staves..."
All arise from the four great elements;
they have never caused injury or harm to earth, water, fire, or wind.
Even if his body were dismembered limb by limb,
his mind would remain ever unmoved;
he knows that the mind does not abide within.
Nor do they arise from without;
all phenomena perish moment by moment,
for their nature never remains established.
Within this, there is neither revilement nor reverence.
Ninth, regarding the distinction between universal and restricted [application]:
While all other precepts have exceptions,
this one alone does not;
this is because the obstruction to the Path caused by anger is so profound.
If one constantly cultivates the antidote,
it merely counteracts the faults of the object and mindfulness;
this is according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
There is no offense;
there is no further allowance.
If one relies on the secret [teachings].
In the *Liang-lun*, it is stated that even Bodhisattvas give rise to anger,
because they rebuke the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the tenth, the explanation of the text:
The four meanings are the same as before:
first, the enumeration of the fault;
second, the formal regulation.
Third, the transgressions;
fourth, the determination of the offense.
In the first [of these], the offenses of oneself and others are raised separately.
Furthermore, it applies to four stages.
Regarding the four explanations of the causal conditions of karma, they are the same as before.
Second, from "And the Bodhisattva... onwards, the correct regulation is clarified.
First, the practice of benefiting others is clarified.
This refers to causing sentient beings to give rise to the wholesome root of non-anger, which is why it is called "the matter of non-contention" (*araṇa*).
Furthermore, it means ensuring that within those wholesome roots there is no occurrence of anger, strife, or contention.
"One who constantly gives rise to a compassionate mind" means that,
by virtue of the intention to benefit others,
one regards them with great compassion and pity as if they were oneself.
How could one possibly give rise to anger?
Third, regarding the subsequent clarification of transgressions, there are three parts:
first, clarifying the object of anger.
This refers to the two objects: sentient and non-sentient beings.
Second, to clarify the karmic function of hatred:
it refers to verbal karma manifested through verbal abuse.
Having dispatched the karma of body,
one does not cease generating the karma of mind.
Third, this clarifies that the anger of the person before is deep and heavy.
This means that because resentment is difficult to relinquish, it is called "unresolved.
The four resulting offenses can be understood [from the text]. 10.

The Precept Against Slandering the Triple Gem. Regarding the first section, the Tenth Precept Against Slandering the Triple Gem: the initial intent for its establishment is briefly due to ten reasons.
First, because no other single course of action is more grave than this;
second, because it incinerates the roots of virtue without exception;
and third, because it is the ultimate among evils for its betrayal of kindness and virtue.
Fourth, because it destroys faith and extinguishes the eye of the Dharma;
fifth, because it causes all virtuous practices, whether small or great, to fail to be accomplished;
sixth, because it leads one into the net of the false views of non-Buddhist paths.
Seventh, because it constitutes a great false view that severs the roots of goodness;
eighth, because it acts as an evil friend to all sentient beings;
ninth, because this view cuts off the lineage of the Three Jewels.
Tenth, because it causes oneself and others to accomplish the karma for the Avīci Hell;
therefore, it is proscribed.
Second, as for the explanation of its name:
Because their supreme virtues are worthy of being treasured, they are called the Three Jewels (*triratna*).
Because it is unreasonable and defiles them with dust, it is termed "slander" (*ābhyākhyāna*).
Since the precepts guard against this fault, they take this as their name.
Regarding the third sequence:
it follows because anger is preceded by wrong view.
Fourth, there are five conditions for its completion.
First, a group of people;
second, the objects of the Three Jewels;
third, the arising of the perception of those three.
Fourth, performing wrong views;
fifth, uttering words of slander, at which point one commits the offense.
Regarding the fifth deficiency of conditions:
If the first condition is lacking, it is not a grave preparatory offense regarding non-sentient objects.
If the second condition is lacking, it is a grave preparatory offense because the object is not the Triple Gem.
If the third condition is lacking, there is no offense as one was fundamentally deluded.
The transformation of thought and doubt both constitute preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
If the fourth condition is lacking, because it does not destroy the view, it constitutes repeated preparatory effort.
If the fifth condition is lacking—meaning that the words have not yet been uttered or that different words were used—it constitutes repeated preparatory effort.
Regarding the sixth [category], the light and heavy [offenses], there are six [factors]:
first, with respect to the person addressed;
second, with respect to the subject of the slander.
Third, in terms of the slanderer;
fourth, in terms of the damage inflicted;
fifth, a combined analysis.
Sixth, regarding oneself and others:
at the beginning, one addresses a single person, two people, many people, or a great assembly;
the former cases are lighter, while the latter are more serious.
Second, regarding the objects of slander,
there are three kinds of Triple Gem:

Question: The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
"When a bodhisattva hears praise of the Buddha or disparagement of the Buddha, their mind remains fixed and unmoved within the Buddha-dharma."
Why is it said here that [this person] is like a spear piercing the heart?
The answer is: there are four types of sentient beings;
first, those who hear the disparagement of the Buddha and feel joy.
Because of their wrong views,
they possess neither joy nor sorrow;
for they are outsiders to the Buddha-dharma.
Third, having heard it, they experience pain,
because they are disciples at the initial stage.
Fourth, having heard it, they are neither sorrowful nor joyful.
Because these are non-retrogressive bodhisattvas;
because they know that the Buddha’s merit cannot be disparaged;
and because disparagement does not reach them.
That sutra is based on the stage of non-retrogression,
whereas this text concerns the initial mind; therefore, they are not the same.

If one who is at the initial stage of practice forcibly conforms to a later stage and no longer feels acute pain, this is an ignorant and evil person who, following their original evil views, endures these matters; therefore, it is not permissible.
Question: Since all phenomena are empty, why is it necessary to exert effort regarding suffering?

Thirdly, it clarifies the transgression through the words spoken by oneself.

Second, one should not violate even a single of the ten precepts,

Within this, there are two parts:

Among the preceding [categories], the first constitutes a loss of the Great Mind (*mahācitta*);

Second is the loss of royal status.

it means that one who violates this precept should enter hell.

2. Section on Minor Defilements (Ling-gou-zui-pian), Second. To explain this section, eight topical gates will be briefly established:
first, the intent of the regulation;
second, the definition of the names.
Third, the category of enumeration;
fourth, the inclusion of both light and heavy [offenses];
fifth, the inclusion of many [factors].
Sixth, the nature of prohibitions;
seventh, the coarse and the subtle;
eighth, the explanation of the text.
Regarding the original intent of the initial formulation:
for what reason did the Buddhas establish these minor precepts?
It is said that the first was to protect the world from giving rise to censure and suspicion.
Second, because it illuminates the path for bodhisattvas to appear in the world;
third, because it completely restrains and severs all subtle sensory objects and afflictions;
fourth, because it subdues the three karmas and controls the three poisons.
Fifth, because it provides distant protection for the ten grave precepts through the five expedient means.
Sixth, because it increases the bodhisattva’s threefold aggregate of precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*).
The remainder is as explained in the commentary on the text below.
Second, regarding the explanation of the names:
"light defilements" (laghu-mala) distinguish these from the previously mentioned heavy precepts;
for this reason, they are called "light."
It is also called "defilement" (mala) because it distinguishes itself from the absence of transgression.
Furthermore, another explanation states that it is called "defilement" because it soils and stains pure conduct.
If the substance is not heavy but one weighs it as light,
or if one who maintains the stage of virtuous precepts (*śīlabhūmi*) violates a minor precept, it is collectively termed *duṣkṛta*.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, this is translated as "evil-doing" (*akaraṇīya*).
It is called *kaukṛtya* (remorse) because it consists of performing what is not in accordance with reason;
furthermore, it is called "action" (*kṛta*) because it is performed with faulty conduct,
and it is also referred to as "evil speech" (*durukta*).
This refers to verbal transgression.
The *Śraddhākarman-sūtra* calls it the offense of "losing one's mind" (*yi-shi*).
This means that because one forgets what has been done and acts contrary to one's original intention, it is termed "losing one's mind."
Regarding the three categories of enumeration, these apply generally to this chapter.
There are ten such categories in this chapter.
First, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
There are forty-four kinds of minor precepts.
Second, according to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śīla-sūtra*,
although there are slight additions and subtractions, it is largely the same as the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
The above mostly constitute the characteristics of the precepts for those who have left the household life.
Third, according to the *Bodhisattvādhyāśaya-śīla-sūtra*,
there are forty-two kinds.
Fourth, according to the *Sūtra on the Origin of Goodness*,
there are twenty-eight precepts in addition to the six grave offenses.
Fifth, according to the Vaipulya Sūtras.
Apart from the twenty-four kinds of precepts, there are additionally five sets of five, totaling twenty-five kinds,
which are prescribed as things that should not be done;
for the most part, those listed above are the precepts for laypeople.
Sixth, based on this sūtra,
there are approximately forty-eight types.
Seventh, if one examines the fine details within this text:
Alternatively, there may be many types of precepts within a single precept;
taken collectively, they number nearly one hundred.
All those mentioned above pertain to the precepts common to both monastics and laypeople.
There are eight or eighty thousand types, as listed below;

such as cited in the Liang dynasty treatise from the *Vinayakṣudraka-sūtra*.
The Bodhisattva precepts have one hundred thousand varieties of distinctions.
As stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, there are ten precepts with as many distinctions as atoms in the sands of the Ganges;
briefly, there are eighty thousand, and extensively, there are as many as the number of atoms in the sands of the Ganges.
All such cases as these belong to this category. Regarding the fourfold classification of light and heavy:
among these forty-eight types, how many are exclusively light, and how many are associated with the heavy?
That is to say, six precepts involve grave offenses;
the remainder are the opposite.
This refers to the precept against killing when acting as an envoy for a state.
Within this context, they are included in this chapter because they act as the driving forces [for further transgression].

thus, they are treated within the precept against setting fires.
Because it involves burning, it is included in this section;

Third, regarding the precept against forcibly begging from officials.
To enter this section by relying on official power and forcibly taking property constitutes an offense against the precept against stealing;
it is included within the fourth category, the precepts concerning one's master.
Failing in decorum as a leader falls under this section;
because it damages the property of the Triple Gem, it is appropriate that it constitute a grave offense.
Fifth, engaging in prohibited conduct is not included among the precepts.
Because he feigned intimacy and so forth, he is included in this section.
Because he himself slandered the Triple Gem, he is included among the grave offenses.

If one commits an offense on the six fasting days or during the three months of the long retreat not for a specific reason, it is included in this section;
because killing is a grave matter,

Using light weights, small measures, and the like are included in this section;
taking another's property and so forth constitutes a grave offense.

Eighth, the explanation of the text:
Within this section, the text is divided into three parts:
first, concluding the preceding and introducing what follows;
second, the formal exposition of the characteristics of the precepts.
Third, the exhortation to practice and study.
First, the preceding section is concluded:
the ten grave precepts have already been explained.
Regarding the subsequent section on the thirty-eight types of light [offenses], which will be explained later,
