1. The Precept on Disrespecting Teachers and Elders. Regarding the first precept on disrespecting teachers and elders, there will be a brief exposition in eight sections:
first, the intent of the precept;
second, the sequence.
Third, the explanation of names;
fourth, the presence of conditions;
fifth, the absence of conditions.
Sixth, lightness and heaviness;
seventh, penetration and obstruction;
eighth, the explanation of the text.
Regarding the original intent of the regulation:
it is the principle that a bodhisattva ought to be humble and reverently support all sentient beings;
how much more so should they never show even the slightest disrespect toward their teachers and elders?
Because such violations of conduct are so extreme, they must be restrained.
Second, regarding the sequence:
once one has newly obtained the precepts...
In principle, one must receive instruction from a teacher;
if one harbors contempt or arrogance, there will be no way for the teaching to proceed.
Therefore, it is necessary to establish this precept first.
Because one relies on the extensive practice of the precepts to easily establish them;
third, the explanation of the names:
Regarding teachers and elders, one might harbor a light mind and physical arrogance;
the precept prevents this fault,
and its name is derived from that which it avoids.
Regarding the four conditions for being complete: they possess four conditions.
First, the person is a teacher, an elder, and a virtuous individual.
Second, one knows that this person is a teacher and so forth.
Third, because one gives rise to contempt;
fourth, because one does not respectfully provide for [the teacher's] body—
therefore, the offense is established.
Regarding the five deficiencies of conditions:
if the first two conditions are deficient,
there is a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) in both cases, because one must show respect toward all sentient beings.
If the third condition is lacking, one incurs a middle offense,
because of a lack of physical and mental respect toward the preceptor.
If the fourth condition is lacking, one incurs a grave offense.
Because of giving rise to a mind of contempt toward one's teachers and elders,
the sixth [category of] lightness and heaviness has four types.
First, regarding the object, there are three grades.
First, one regards the two teachers as most important;
second, one regards the elders and those of seniority next;
third, one regards those of the same class.
Regarding these three objects, it should be understood that the three grades of offenses—superior, middling, and inferior—are incurred.
Second, with respect to the mind, there are likewise three grades:
namely, first, committing a superior offense with a mind of resentment or a mind of malice.
Second, the absence of resentment and so forth, arising solely from pride and delusion, constitutes the medium degree.
Third, laziness and forgetfulness constitute the inferior degree.
These three are correlated with the preceding three objects in their respective order.
The intermingling of light and heavy [degrees of gravity] can be understood.
Fourth, regarding the matter itself, there are also three grades:
first, those who are unable to sell their own bodies and so forth.
Second, failing to provide respectful offerings in accordance with the Dharma;
third, failing to welcome, see off, or prostrate.
The three grades of offenses—lower, middle, and upper—may be understood accordingly.
Seventh, regarding the penetration of obstructions:
first, not recognizing [the object] in the darkness of night;
second, when one is asleep yet perceives the signs of another's activity as being awake.
Third, if one has a serious illness;
fourth, if one has recently recovered from an illness and lacks strength;
fifth, if one is seated while preaching the Dharma.
Sixth, if one listens to the Dharma correctly and protects the mind of the teacher of the Dharma,
one commits no transgressions, as explained in the *Yogācāra-śīla*.
Regarding the eighth section, the explanation of the text, there are three phrases.
First, it clarifies the receiving and attaining of the precepts;
second, from "once attained" onwards, it demonstrates the practice and exhorts one to maintain them.
This also serves as the preceding section for the reception of the precepts.
This constitutes the secondary offense (*anuvartana*).
If it were not as stated above, it would contradict the concluding summary of the offenses; thus, there are two [offenses] regarding the first and the initial [cases].
First, the stages for receiving the precepts shall be clarified.
Briefly stated, there are three such stages.
The first is the king, including those who rule over minor principalities and the like.
Second, the two ministers of state for gold, silver, copper,
and iron; third, the three high officials who oversee all civil and military affairs—
these are the three noble ranks.
One is able to both harm and benefit all sentient beings;
if one does not receive the precepts, the spirits will not provide protection.
How, then, can one govern the multitude of living beings?
Therefore, it is said that one should first receive the bodhisattva precepts.
Second, the section beginning with "All those below" clarifies the benefits of receiving the precepts;
this accords with the intention of the Sages.
The Buddhas rejoice; below,
they harmonize with the myriad spirits, who provide ghostly protection so that their bodies shall be free from calamity and their positions shall endure forever.
The second section, "Showing the Practice for Upholding," also has two parts:
first, the positive demonstration of what should be practiced;
second, from "However, the bodhisattva... onwards, the negative deviations.
This demonstrates that it is not any of the three [stages] mentioned previously:
first, the arising of a heavy mind;
second, seeing a person of honor.
Third, regarding the ritual of showing reverence,
there are two initial mental states:
namely, repaying kindness through respectful service, and reverently following the commands of one’s superior as an act of filial piety.
There are three kinds of reverence:
first, service; second, welcoming and seeing off.
Third, prostrations.
Furthermore, these two types of mind are also the constant practices of a bodhisattva.
Regarding the "two venerable persons," they are briefly categorized as six kinds of people.
First, the *sthavira*, who is the foremost among the assembly;
second, the *upādhyāya* (also called *upādhyāya*), which in this [language] is translated as "Preceptor" (*qīn jiàoshī*).
However, there are three kinds:
first, the preceptor for the ten precepts;
second, the preceptor for full ordination.
The third, the preceptor for bodhisattva precepts,
is none other than the Buddhas. Here,
however, we refer to the former two.
Regarding the mention of the three *ācāryas*,
this is translated as "masters of discipline" (*kǔifàn zhī shī*).
It is so named because they provide instruction in the rules and methods [of practice].
However, there are six types:
first, the preceptor for the ten precepts;
second, the ritual master for the full ordination.
Third, instruction on the three modes of deportment;
fourth, receiving the formal practice; fifth, the basis of reliance;
sixth, the bestowal of the bodhisattva precepts.
The four kinds of fellow students refer to those who study the Bodhisattva-piṭaka under the same teacher, such as those who are senior in years or summer retreats.
The fifth is having the same view.
Sixth, common practice (*samāna-pratipatti*).
This refers to sharing the same view regarding the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka teachings and practicing the same conduct as that practiced by bodhisattvas.
The former refers to sameness of understanding;
the latter refers to sameness of practice.
These two apply both to those with the same teacher and those with different teachers.
However, those who share these same karmic actions are all equally esteemed.
Furthermore, this explanation also applies to those of the Hīnayāna who follow the path of understanding and practice;
they too are all equally esteemed.
Because they likewise belong within the same Buddha-dharma,
there are three points regarding the ritual of showing respect:
if one is ill, one should rise.
If one lacks the strength, one should receive [the guest] by advancing to meet them;
if one is in good health, one should perform prostrations.
Furthermore, this explains that first one rises, next one welcomes, and finally one pays homage.
Second, the bodhisattva’s failure to conform to and lose [the path].
This reveals that it is not the middle two.
First, the failure is presented.
This means that arrogance (*māna*) is the opposite of the aforementioned mind of reverence;
delusion (*moha*) is the opposite of the mind of filial piety,
resulting in a lack of filiality toward one's teacher.
To show disrespect toward those who are superior,
or to possess both of the former two [pride and arrogance],
and furthermore, to be disrespectful toward those above oneself, is called *mada* (haughtiness).
To consider oneself equal to those who are superior is pride (*māna*);
to possess both of the aforementioned [states] is delusion (*moha*).
This is a mind that acts in opposition [to the path].
"Not rising to meet them" and so forth are signs of contrary conduct;
each of these has two types.
First, regarding each individual among the six classes of persons mentioned previously, one fails to provide offerings and so forth in accordance with the Dharma;
second, regarding each specific act of offering performed for those persons, each fails to accord with the Dharma.
There are three types of offerings:
first, the offering of reverence,
which refers to acts such as welcoming and prostrating.
Second is material offering,
which refers to incense, flowers, and so forth.
Third is the offering of practice.
This refers to practicing according to the teachings and so forth;
all three of these factors must be fully possessed.
This will be clarified below in the section on the protocol of reverence.
Since it is never permitted for one who is destitute and lacks the means to provide offerings,
this present case of selling one's own body as an act of discipline applies to both the state of the layperson and the state of the renunciant.
To sell one’s country, city, and royal throne:
that which is governed is called a "country" (guó),
and that which is occupied is called a "city" (chéng).
Those who are sold are the sons and daughters [of the Buddha] according to his original vow;
therefore, there is no fault in selling them.
Furthermore, this Bodhisattva values people and values practice.

Because their affection is so profound, they break through this bond of love and affection; ultimately, they do not share the same worldly aspirations, and even men and women sever their passions to turn toward the Dharma.
These two positions refer to laypeople.
The "seven treasures" refers to the rank of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin).

"Various things" refers to all that exists and so forth.
Among these, regarding the seven treasures and the various things, there are two meanings.

The Precept Against Drinking Alcohol. Regarding the second precept, the original intent of its formulation was that alcohol is a drug that causes confusion and madness;
grave faults arise because of it.
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* contains thirty-six faults,
while the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that one can commit four of the ānantarya crimes,
with the sole exception of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
Because this is an extreme transgression, it must be regulated.
Regarding the sequence: the preceding section revealed a lack of external decorum;
the present section clarifies that there is no internal confusion, and thus it follows next.
Third, regarding the explanation of the name: it is also established based on what is prohibited.
Fourth, regarding the requisites:
first, it must be alcohol.
Second, having the perception of it as such;
third, not being afflicted by a serious illness;
fourth, drinking it constitutes an offense.
Question: In the Vinaya of the Hīnayāna, drinking alcohol is not permitted even when there is doubt or a mistaken perception.
Why, then, is that same perception [of intoxication] mentioned here?
Answer: Because alcohol is the source of all transgressions.
That [text] does not mention confusion and so forth;
rather, it refers to the full perception based on the conditions for its formation.
Therefore, the text says: "If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally drinks alcohol."
Since it is stated that drinking intentionally constitutes a clear offense,
one who drinks unintentionally does not incur a formal transgression.
Regarding the five deficiencies of conditions:
If the first condition is lacking, a minor offense is incurred because of the arising of conceptualization and so forth;
if the second condition is lacking, a middling offense is incurred.
Because the object is real,
it should be understood that if the third or fourth [factors] are missing, there is no offense.
Regarding the sixth [factor], lightness and heaviness, there are three [distinctions].
If judged by the object,
diluted wine and the like should be considered light offenses, while strong liquor should be considered heavy.
Second, if judged by the mind.
If the offense is minor, there is no greed, and it is also committed lightly, it should be considered light;
the opposite should be considered heavy.
Third, in terms of the object.
If one induces [the recipient] to drink something of minor benefit and they drink it together, the offense is light;
the opposite case is also grave.
Seventh, regarding penetration and obstruction:
If one drinks alcohol for the sake of saving a life from danger and the like, there is no offense—
as in the case of Queen Mallikā and others.
Furthermore, if one drinks together with another to save them from the karma of the immediate retributions (*ānantarya-karma*), it is to encourage them to cease their coarse and heavy actions.
In principle, there is no offense.
Conversely, all that is done contrary to this constitutes an offense.
Eighth, regarding the explanation of the text, there are also four parts.
First, the title indicates the gravity of the offense regarding alcohol;
second, the section beginning with "If one [drinks] oneself" explains and establishes its gravity;
third, the section beginning with "One must not instruct others" correctly prescribes what is prohibited as grave.
Fourth, regarding the offense incurred through intentional and repeated transgression:

as for the statement at the beginning that "the faults of alcohol are immeasurable," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* lists thirty-six types; this is a brief indication, and they should be enumerated in full.
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, fascicle fifteen, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"In general, there are ten faults in drinking alcohol.
What are these ten?"
First, the complexion is poor;
second, strength is diminished;
third, vision is unclear.
Fourth, manifesting thoughts of anger and hatred;
fifth, destroying fields, occupations, and the means of livelihood;
sixth, increasing and bringing about illness.
Seventh, they increase strife and litigation.
Eighth, they lack a good reputation and an evil name spreads abroad.
Ninth, their wisdom diminishes.
Tenth, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life,
one falls into the evil realms. Furthermore, for example, while the bhikṣu Sāgata was previously able to subdue venomous nāgas,
later, due to drinking alcohol, he was unable to subdue even frogs and the like.
Furthermore, the Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī Sūtra states:
"One must not drink alcohol;
one must not taste alcohol."
One must not smell alcohol;
one must not sell alcohol;
one must not give alcohol to others to drink.
One must not claim to be ill as a pretext to drink medicinal wine.
One must not go to a tavern.
One must not converse with those who frequent taverns.
Alcohol is a poisonous medicine;
alcohol is a poisonous water;
alcohol is a poisonous vapor.
It is the source of all losses and the root of all evils;
it harms the worthy and slanders the sages, bringing ruin to the Way and its Virtue.
By slighting and disparaging others, it invites calamity and establishes the foundation of disaster.
The decay of the four great elements and the departure from merit toward transgression do not fail to arise from this.
It would be better to drink molten copper than to drink the taste of alcohol.
Why is this? Because alcohol causes one to lose their resolve, become deluded and confused, and fall into madness.
It causes people to enter the hells without even realizing it;
therefore, one must guard against alcohol.
Other failings are as explained in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
In the second section, the explanation and establishment, there are two parts.
First, the minor [retribution] is cited:
for five hundred lifetimes, one shall be without hands.
Master Dushun’s commentary explains:
"Because both are feet, it is said that there are no hands;
this refers precisely to animals."
Second, as for "let alone those who drink themselves," this is an even more weighty case.
Third, within the actual prohibition (*vidhi*), it likewise first cites the case of others and subsequently uses it to illustrate the case of oneself.
Regarding the former [the citation of others], "all sentient beings" refers to...
One must not allow even animals and the like to drink [the water],
for this would result in the failure to benefit others; thus,
it should be understood that one commits an offense by violating the formal precept.
3. The Precept Against Eating Meat, Third. Regarding the original intent of this initial regulation:
it is the principle that a Bodhisattva should rationally sacrifice their own flesh to save the lives of other beings.
How could one possibly consume the flesh of sentient beings?
Because such an act is an extreme violation and harm, it must be prohibited.
Second, as for the sequence:
Previously, one abstained from intoxicating drinks that cause confusion;
now, one abstains from food that harms life.
This is because they follow in sequence.
Third, regarding the explanation of the name:
consuming the bodily parts of sentient beings in an irrational manner is called "eating meat.
This precept is established by its name based on the function of preventing this transgression.
The four [types of meat] possess four conditions:
first, it must be human flesh, because there is no offense in consuming non-human flesh;
second, it must be the flesh of another, because there is no formal offense in eating one's own flesh.
Third, the perception of it as meat arises;
because this is an error, there is no offense.
Fourth, the moment it enters the mouth, an offense is committed.
Because there is no fault in not eating,
the five deficiencies of conditions can be understood.
Regarding the sixth, lightness and gravity, there are four [factors].
First, in terms of the object;
second, in terms of the mental state;
third, a combined analysis.
Fourth, regarding the defilements:
within the first category of objects, there are four types.
First, the flesh of livestock that is still in the womb or covered by the placenta is meat devoid of life.
Second, meat from animals that died of themselves;
third, the three kinds of pure meat;
fourth, knowing that the animal was killed for one's sake, and so forth.
Regarding the precepts, all are transgressed;
as for the paths of karma, they are respectively light in the former and heavy in the latter. Second, regarding the mental states, there are also three [degrees].
First, medicine for a grave illness;
second, sustenance for life during a famine;
third, regular food for one who is negligent.
They likewise both violate the precepts;
the paths of action (karmapatha) should be understood accordingly. Regarding the three combined explanations, the subsequent items are to be paired with the preceding ones in their respective order.
The interconnections of light and heavy [karmas] are to be understood by analogy. Fourth, regarding the afflictions, the three poisons are to be understood by analogy.
Seventh, regarding penetration and obstruction, this is in relation to oneself.
It is entirely obstructed and lacks any passage; yet,
with respect to the mind that transforms sentient beings,
there exists the condition for causing them to resolve upon bodhicitta.
Although the explicit text has not yet been seen, by inference it should also apply here.
Regarding the eightfold explanation of the text, there are three phrases;
the first raises the offense.
Second, the formal regulation;
third, the determination of the offense.
Within the formal regulation, there are two parts.
First, the prohibition is established:
"all meat" refers generally to the physical constituents of the four modes of birth.
Second, from "severing great compassion" downward, the intent of the prohibition is explained and established by means of the three faults.
First, one severs the failure to transform others due to a lack of compassion.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Those who eat meat sever the seeds of great loving-kindness and great compassion."
This eating of meat violates and harms the nature of great compassion, thereby forfeiting one's own benefit;
when sentient beings see such abandonment, they lose the opportunity for the benefit of others.
Furthermore, it first contravenes the cause of transformation and subsequently forfeits the fruit of transformation.
It is further said that when animals see a person who eats meat, they perceive a glow of blood upon the person's head and think:
My body has flesh;
that person eats flesh.
If he were to obtain me, he would surely eat me.
I then became terrified and fled.
As it is extensively stated in such texts as the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the *Aṅguli-mālīya Sūtra*,
and as is fully revealed regarding the faults of eating meat in the *Sarvajñāprabha-ṛṣi-amāṃsabhakṣaṇa-hetu-pratyaya-sūtra*.
That rishi was none other than Maitreya Bodhisattva,
who shall attain Buddhahood in the future;
he established the prohibition against eating meat as a grave offense.
It is exactly as stated there.
Second, all bodhisattvas below [this level] incur the fault of non-human transgressions.
This refers to those who have generally resolved upon the bodhicitta and practice the conduct of a bodhisattva.
One ought to sacrifice one's own life to save sentient beings;
how could one instead eat the flesh of sentient beings?
Therefore, this is improper.
Third, eating meat incurs immeasurable minor offenses and grave losses; that is to say,
according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*,
eating meat constitutes the offense of taking life.
Because one accepts and approves of the killing of living beings.
Furthermore, as it is said:
"Meat does not arise spontaneously."
All [meat] is obtained by taking life.
If a person does not abstain from meat,
they are a thief who robs others of their lives.
The third offense may be understood as before.

Regarding the fourth precept on abstaining from the five pungent vegetables: the original intent of this initial regulation was that a Bodhisattva ought, by principle, to abide in fragrance and purity.
Conversely, eating such pungent and defiled food causes a foul stench to billow forth, causing the worthy sages and celestial deities to abandon and distance themselves from it;
therefore, it must be regulated.
Regarding the sequence:
previously one consumed that which possessed life;
now, one commits the offense of consuming that which lacks life, and thus it is sequential.
Third, regarding the explanation of the names:
that which is foul-smelling and pungent is called *kaṭu*.
According to the distinctions among its numerical categories, there are five types.
Improper consumption constitutes eating;
the precept is established to prevent this fault,
and its name is likewise derived from its function.
The four [factors] possess four conditions:
first, the five pungent herbs;
second, the perception of them as such.
Third, there are circumstances where no offense is incurred, namely: being afflicted by a serious illness, or engaging in activities such as saving sentient beings.
Fourth, an offense is committed immediately after having finished eating.
The five absences of conditions may be inferred accordingly.
Sixth, regarding gravity:
it depends on whether the influence of the object is intense or faint.
In terms of mental states, there is craving and aversion;
in terms of objective conditions, there is harm and benefit.
In both cases, their relative gravity can be discerned.
Regarding the seventh point, "permeability and obstruction":
this refers to circumstances such as one's own serious illness or the necessity of saving many sentient beings for their benefit and peace;
in principle, these should be considered permeable.
All others are obstructions.
Within the eighth section, "Explanation of the Text," there are three parts.
First is the general regulation.
The second [category], garlic, is separately regulated.
Here, the five pungent vegetables (pañca-garaka) differ from those in other places;
in other places, leeks, scallions, onions, garlic, and asafoetida constitute the five.
Among these five items mentioned in this text, garlic can be identified.
Some say that *ci-cōng* (慈葱) is the same as *hú-cōng* (胡葱).
*Lán-cōng* (lancong) is domestic onion;
the first three types are common foods of the human world;
*gé-cōng* (gecong) is mountain onion.
This exists in the northern regions but not in the south.
Regarding its *xingqu* (興渠):
some say it is *yuntai* (芸臺).
However, no authentic textual evidence has yet been seen.
Some say that in Jiangnan there is a plant with leaves resembling those of wild garlic.
The roots and stems resemble those of leeks;
it is also called *piluizi*.
It bears no seeds and is not found in northern regions.
Furthermore, it is explained that the Sanskrit name for the medicinal herb *arvuda* is *hiṅgu*.
It was thought that this [plant] was the sprout or leaf of that pungent and foul-smelling substance.

Chapter Five: On Not Exposing Faults and Teaching Repentance for Precepts. Regarding the original intent of this initial regulation:
it is the principle that a Bodhisattva ought to expose the transgressions of others to them, causing them to repent and purify themselves, so as to ensure they attain complete purity.
He commissioned this work to be sent as a legacy so that the True Dharma would not decline for a thousand years;
to rescue the common people below by never abandoning any living beings,
and to protect the holy teachings above as a way of repaying the Buddha’s kindness.

As for the sequence of the two [practices]:

The Noble One’s establishment of the precepts was for the purpose of preventing the fault of being biased by personal affection, concealing another's transgression, and failing to exhort them toward repentance;
the precepts serve as a safeguard against such failings.
The name is also established based on its functional capacity.
Regarding the fourth point, "possessing conditions":

If the first two [conditions] are lacking, there is no offense;

That is to say, if by raising the matter against them, they would immediately give rise to afflictions.

therefore, they are like grass spread upon the ground.

Regarding the six points on lightness and gravity:

Furthermore, failing to report [a transgression] out of negligence constitutes a grave offense; likewise, failing to report it because one's merit is weak and unable to do so constitutes a light offense;

if one lacks the five virtues oneself and others do not follow, [one's teaching will be obstructed].

Second, the eightfold explanation of the text has two parts.

second, the violation of that regulation by a bodhisattva.

The Sixth Precept: Not Respecting Those Who Request the Dharma. The Sixth Precept: Not Respecting Those Who Request the Dharma.
Regarding the original intent of this regulation:
that which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma.
It is only logical that a Bodhisattva should revere the person and honor the Dharma, even to the point of sacrificing one's body in seeking and requesting it.
On the contrary, they instead sit with their legs exposed in a haughty and arrogant manner, showing contempt for people and the Dharma.
Because this is an extreme loss of the Way, it must be regulated.
Second, as for the sequence:
Previously, one did not provide instruction to those who had fallen away;
now, one does not respectfully request [teachings] from those who have attained them.
Third, the explanation of the names:
To treat others with contempt and to be negligent toward the Dharma is called "disrespectful invitation.
The precept prevents this fault;
thus, it is also named according to its functional efficacy.
Regarding the four conditions for the full completion of the offense: there are four conditions that constitute a transgression.
First, there must actually be a person who possesses both the understanding and the practice of the Mahāyāna.
Second, there is no distinct opening of conditions;
third, one consequently gives rise to a conceited mind;
fourth, one fails to make offerings and does not request the Dharma.
The five absences of conditions can be understood [as previously explained].
Regarding the sixth point, lightness and heaviness,
there are three types when categorized by person.
First, regarding those who have transcended the stage of conduct through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*):
although these preceptors (*ācārya*) may be arrogant and lack respect, it is indeed appropriate that they be honored when requested [to teach].
Second, if those whose understanding and practice are equal to one's own do not request [instruction], it is minor and slight.
Third, if those inferior to oneself do not request, there is no offense.
Second, regarding the Dharma, there are likewise three cases.
One may understand this by analogy with other persons.
Regarding the seventh point, "Penetration and Obstruction," the *Jieling* (Vinaya Sūtra) on the "Multi-storied Tower" states:
If a bodhisattva, out of a mind of pride, fails to consult a teacher or receive the teacher’s instruction,
they incur an offense.
There is no offense if they are ill, insane, or deluded.
If one who is of great intelligence, extensive learning, and wisdom enters meditative concentration for the sake of disciplining sentient beings—
this is the eighth explanation of the text.
The text consists of three parts.
First, seeing a superior person coming from afar clarifies the conditions for establishing the precepts.
Second, "immediately rising," etc., clarifies the actual establishment of the precepts.
Third, if it were not so, it would contradict the conclusion of the clarification.
Regarding the phrase "first, a Mahāyāna Dharma Master" at the beginning:
this is a general enumeration intended to distinguish [the subject] from the Hīnayāna.
The distinctions are explained below.
They are identical regarding the Great Dharma; they are identical in that their views and understandings are superior.
"Practicing together" refers to the excellence of practice.
"Entering the monastic quarters" refers to ordained bodhisattvas;

Regarding the cities and towns, this concerns the king and others.
Within the two sections on formal regulations,
the first concerns the people who provide respect and support.
Second, the method for requesting instruction through formal invitation:
the acts of welcoming and escorting at the beginning and end involve observing the ritual deportment of the initial and final stages;

The Precept on Not Attending to the Suffering of Illness. Regarding the ninth precept, "The Precept on Not Attending to the Suffering of Illness," the original intent of its initial formulation is as follows:
The Bodhisattva takes great compassion as his essence and the uprooting of suffering as his function;
how could he bear to see illness and yet fail to provide care and rescue?
Therefore, it must be regulated.
Furthermore, if one can restrain the mind while nursing the patient so that they may recover,
this itself constitutes the severing of [one's own] life.
Therefore, it is necessary to establish these regulations.
Furthermore, if even the Tathāgata, the Great Sage, personally attended to the suffering of illness,
how much more so should others provide care and rescue?
Regarding the two stages:
previously one relied on superior dharmas;
now, one abandons the inferiority of illness and suffering.
Therefore, it is regulated next.
Furthermore, previously one was contrary to the Dharma;
now one fails to rescue sentient beings.
Therefore, it is established next.
Third, regarding the explanation of the names:
illness and suffering are adjacent to the calamity of death.
To abandon them and fail to rescue them truly violates the practice of compassion; yet,
by establishing prohibitions to prevent [such harm],
one likewise earns the title of being effective.
Regarding the four conditions:
first, the suffering of illness;
second, the perception thereof.
Third, [the offense occurs] when one is free from illness and so forth;
fourth, when one abandons [the patient] out of a mind of aversion.
Therefore, these constitute the completion of the offense.
Regarding the five absences of conditions:
if the first two conditions are absent, there is no offense.
Among the absences of the third condition:
If one abandons [the patient] because they themselves have been ill for some time,
one incurs a minor offense (duṣkṛta);
if the illness is severe, there is no offense.
Regarding the fourth condition among the omissions:
if one departs with a mind of resentment without relinquishing [the object], or if one departs with a mind of compassion while relinquishing it,
in both cases one incurs a minor offense (duṣkṛta).
As stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and other sources:

The Tenth Precept: Prohibiting the Possession of Various Instruments of Killing. Regarding the original intent of this initial regulation:
A Bodhisattva, by principle, ought to extensively gather the wealth of the Dharma to bring benefit and joy to sentient beings.

therefore, they must be regulated.

Previously, one protected oneself but could not cure illness;

Third, regarding the explanation of the name:

Fourth, regarding the complete conditions:

Second, there is the perception that it is [permissible];

Regarding the sixth point, lightness and heaviness:

Regarding the seventh point on obstructions and openings:

Conversely, to keep any of these things is a transgression for all.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva sees another keeping such things, they should urge them to destroy them.
If they cannot be urged to do so, [they should act accordingly].
One should beg for it or redeem it;
yet even if these fail, one should employ methods such as intimidation to investigate and recover it.
It must be brought to a halt.
Regarding the eighth section, the explanation of the text, there are three parts.
First, the prohibition against possessing unsuitable vessels.
Second, ceasing internal enmity;
third, intentionally violating the precepts constitutes an offense.
Regarding the first of these, it refers primarily to the frequent killing of various classes of sentient beings.
Briefly listed, there are ten kinds:
first, the sword, which has the meaning of cutting and severing;
second, the staff, which has the meaning of striking and beating.
The third, *gō* (bow), signifies the meaning of sending forth an arrow;
the fourth, *sha* (arrow), signifies the meaning of striking and harming;
the fifth, *kō* (spear), signifies the meaning of wounding and inflicting judgment.
The sixth, "axes," has the meaning of felling and cutting.
The seventh refers to instruments of combat;
that is to say, armor, crossbows, and so forth—all such items are instruments of war.
The above [categories] generally harm both humans and animals.
The eighth is the net of evil, which refers to fishing and bird-catching.
The ninth is the instrument of killing, which collectively includes pits, traps, and the like.
Tenth, the summary:
Since all things that constitute harm must not be possessed, it says "none at all may be possessed.
Second, from "The Bodhisattva" onwards, it stops internal enmity and demonstrates the practice to be cultivated.
Among them, those who have merely resolved their minds to practice the bodhisattva path may encounter the enmity of having killed their parents;

"To repay enmity with enmity,
the enmity can never be exhausted."
Only when one accords with the absence of enmity will enmity cease;
therefore, one does not retaliate.
How much more so for a Bodhisattva who contemplates all sentient beings?
All those who are without resentment are entirely objects of compassion;
all are equally subjects of loving-kindness and salvation.
Even toward those who have previously been enemies, he arouses a profound mind of reverence and regards them as his own infant.
[The opponent asks: "If that is so, how does a bodhisattva fulfill filial piety toward his own parents?"
The answer is: If one’s parents have not yet been harmed,
even if one were to grind one’s own body into atoms like fine dust for immeasurable eons,
one must still practice filial piety to preserve and nurture them.
If their parents have already been killed,
it is the result of past karma;
to retaliate against them would be of no benefit.
This will further invite great harm, and resentment will never cease,
just as when the Vṛji people were destroyed by the Śākyas;
even the Tathāgata’s supernatural powers could do nothing against it.
This is what is meant.
As for the phrase "let alone other sentient beings," it is an instance of citing a weightier case to illustrate a lighter one.
In terms of the object, the gravity [of the offense] is weighed: it is grave toward one's parents,
and light toward other sentient beings.
Regarding the state of mind:
if one repays a debt of sin for the sake of one's parents, the offense is mitigated;

second, because they are unacquainted with the meaning of the texts.
Because they have lost their virtuous qualities;
and third, because they falsely pose as teachers for others without providing genuine guidance,
thereby failing to benefit them.
These three are, in their respective order, also the three aggregates;
therefore, they must be established.
Second, as for the sequence:
Previously, they used forceful intimidation to seize [the teachings];
now, they feign the transmission of the Dharma.
Therefore, this is explained next.
Third, regarding the explanation of the name:
it conceals one's own ignorance while falsely assuming the role of a teacher;
the precepts prevent this transgression.
Therefore, it is named as such. Regarding the fourth point, the "complete conditions":
an offense is established when four conditions are fulfilled.
First, being of a dull nature;
second, being indolent and not practicing study;
third, being hidden in folly while feigning wisdom.
Fourth, it is considered an offense because the precepts were conferred by a teacher.
Fifth, regarding those who lack the necessary conditions:
If any one of these four conditions is successively lacking,
one incurs a light offense of preliminary preparation (āpatti-śikṣāpada-prayoga).
This may be understood according to the explanation.
Regarding the six cases of light and heavy offenses:
if one actually lacks knowledge yet falsely claims to understand,
this constitutes the offense of lying, which is the first category of transgression.
Now, because [the practitioner] has deviated from the correct guidance and caused the Dharma to be transgressed rather than transmitted,
this offense is established.
Within this, there are six [points].
First, the faculties have degrees of sharpness and dullness;
second, those in training differ in their diligence;
third, concealments vary in their depth.
Regarding the four teachers, there are major and minor [offenses].
Among the five and four [categories], both light and heavy [offenses] exist.
When the six characteristics are combined, they mutually vary in being many or few, and likewise possess both light and heavy [degrees].
This can be understood by applying the same explanation.
Seventh, regarding penetration and obstruction:
if one is by nature dull-witted and has not yet achieved mastery despite diligent study.
If one does not conceal one's ignorance,
or if there is no one to serve as a teacher,
then all such actions should be understood as non-offenses.
The opposite of the above constitutes all violations.
Regarding the eighth section, the explanation of the text, there are also four parts.
First, the presentation of what should correctly be cultivated.
Second, there is no deceptive interpretation;
third, there is no teaching as a master without understanding;
fourth, the formal indication of the name of the offense.
The beginning and middle consist of two parts:
first, one should recite the text;
second, one should cause the meaning to be understood. Within the former, I shall briefly present the general outline.
One should recite and uphold [this] during the six periods;

Next, regarding the explanation of "meaning" (*artha*):

Furthermore, it is explained as the cause for attaining Buddhahood;
therefore, it is called "Buddha-nature.
Briefly, there are three kinds.

Second, from "And the bodhisattva... onwards, it clarifies the absence of ignorance and deception.
Regarding the passage "discerning ignorance, saying one does not understand a single phrase," etc.,

eight characters constitute four phrases.
Four lines constitute one verse.
The origin from which the formulation of the precepts arises is called the causal condition (*nidāna*);

Furthermore, the receiving of the precepts has its causes and conditions,
and the observance of the precepts likewise has its causes and conditions;
all must be thoroughly understood.
Only then is one fit to be a teacher.
Next, there are those who feign understanding;
they conceal their own ignorance while falsely claiming to be able to explain.
Deceiving others and stealing their good reputation—
this below reveals its faults:
namely, that losing one's own true benefit constitutes self-deception.
Not only does he fail to receive benefit, but he also deceives others;

His constant state of complacency and forbearance constitutes a most grievous affliction.
Section 311b clarifies that one who lacks understanding cannot serve as a teacher.
This means that if one does not understand each and every dharma of practice,
then in reality there is nothing understood, yet they nonetheless presume to act as a master or model.
Not only do both the teacher and the disciple deceive themselves and others,
but they also cause the Tathāgata’s Lotus Sūtra to be obstructed from its circulation;

Because the offense is particularly grave, the fourth section below concludes by indicating the name of the transgression, which may be understood accordingly. 19.

The Precept Against Quarreling, Slandering, and Deceiving the Worthy. Regarding the nineteenth precept, "Quarreling, Slandering, and Deceiving the Worthy," the original intent for its establishment is as follows:
A bodhisattva ought, as a matter of principle, to extol and praise those who practice the bodhisattva path,
so that their good reputation may spread far and wide and the common people may emulate them;
yet instead, with malicious intent, they slander, revile, dispute, and destroy them, thereby increasing evil and diminishing goodness.
Because the loss [involved] is grave,
this precept was established;
it is also explained in three distinct parts.
This means that evil does not cease,
goodness does not increase, and one acts contrary to what has been transgressed.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
As for the sequence [of these stages], it was previously explained that they arise from one's own ignorance.
This is because they now deceive those who possess virtue.
Third, regarding the explanation of the names:
they spread slander to incite strife and deceive or despise the worthy and good.
The precepts prevent these faults;
therefore, they are so named.
Fourth, regarding the completeness of conditions:
It possesses five conditions:
first, there is an evil mind within;
second, one sees a person who observes the precepts and practices.
Third, slandering with evil words;
fourth, acting as a go-between for both parties;
fifth, instigating evil to cause strife.
Therefore, an offense is established.
Regarding the five deficiencies of conditions:
if the first condition is deficient, one incurs a light preparatory offense.
Because there was no malicious intent,
the remaining deficiencies all constitute grave preparatory acts;
this may be understood by referring to the commentary.
Regarding the six aspects of lightness and heaviness, there are also ten meanings:
first, the mind encompasses the three natures;
second, the objects involve both observance and violation.
Third, slander has degrees of depth;
fourth, transmission has cases of reaching its destination and not reaching it;
fifth, contention has variations in quantity.
Sixth, both are equally thick.
Seventh, the thick is much and the thin is little.
Eighth, the thin is much and the thick is little.
Ninth, regarding thickness and so forth;
tenth, regarding inequality— all possess degrees of lightness and heaviness,
which may be understood by referring to the commentary.
Regarding the seventh point on obstructions and openings:
if one is mistaken, insane, possessed by a ghost,
or if one is punishing a criminal, there is no offense according to the rule.
Conversely, all the above cases constitute offenses.
Regarding the eighth section on the explanation of the text, there are three parts.
First, [the offense of] viewing a pure object with a wrong view.
The first two constitute an offense by omission;
the third constitutes an offense by commission.
Regarding the first: it is called "an evil mind" because it arises from a mind intent on destruction, a mind of slander, or a mind of envy toward those who excel.
To see a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts as one who has not violated the minor or major rules;
to hold incense and other items in hand as an expression of the dignified deportment of practicing the Path;
and for these two to engage in mutual strife and slander, thereby committing a transgression.
This means that quarreling and contention cause two parties to fall into opposition and dispute;
with a malicious mind to overreach others constitutes deception;
and speaking falsely about their faults constitutes slander.
They slander this person to that person,
and likewise slander that person to this person;
thus they spread mutual slanders to incite strife and contention.
Because of this, evil arises;
thus it is said that "there is no evil one does not create.
Third, as for "if intentionally" and so forth, the conclusion regarding the offense can be understood from the text.
20. The Precept on Not Saving Life from Peril. Regarding the original intent of this precept:
a Bodhisattva, by principle, ought to sacrifice their own life to save others.
Yet, on the contrary, they see the suffering of sentient beings and remain without compassionate rescue;
this is an extreme violation of proper conduct,
and therefore it must be regulated.
To speak of them separately, there are also three:
namely, increasing evil, diminishing good, and failing to save living beings.
Second, regarding their sequence:
Previously, you deceived and slandered the virtuous;
now, seeing their suffering, you do not rescue them.
Third, the explanation of the names:
Lacking internal compassion, one fails to rescue others when seeing their suffering;
the precept guards against this fault,
and thus it is named accordingly.
Regarding the four conditions for completion: there are four conditions.
First, one lacks compassion within.
Second, one sees someone killing a living being.
Third, to abandon them and fail to rescue them;
fourth, to cause their lives to end;
thus, these constitute an offense.
Regarding the five deficiencies of conditions:
the deficiency of the first condition results in a grave preparatory offense,
because although one possesses a compassionate heart, one does not provide rescue.
The absence of the second condition has two meanings.
First, there is no offense in general,
because since one does not see the person who is killing, there is nothing that can be saved.
Second, there is the failure to obtain the heavy preparatory effort (*prayoga*),
because one sees suffering sentient beings yet does not rescue them.
Regarding the deficiency of the third condition, there are also two meanings.
First, there is the minor preparatory effort (*prayoga*),
because although one lacks a compassionate heart, one does not abandon the attempt to save.
Second, there is no offense because the king’s power is so absolute that rescue cannot be achieved.
The fourth condition is absent, whereby one incurs the gravity of the preparatory effort (*prayoga*);
this is because the life-force is not severed by means of rescue.
Other meanings should be inferred accordingly.
Regarding the six aspects of lightness and heaviness, there are six meanings:
first, the distinction between thickness and thinness based on the presence or absence of a compassionate mind;
second, the distinction between honor and lowliness based on the sentient beings to be saved.
Third, regarding the power of the salvific practice performed, it is distinguished by whether that power is attained or not;
fourth, regarding the suffering to be saved from, it is distinguished by whether it is greater or lesser;
fifth, combining these, there are cases of purely light and purely heavy [suffering].
Sixth, light offenses are many and heavy ones few;
seventh, heavy offenses are many and light ones few;
both may be understood by analogy with the preceding cases.
Regarding the seventh point on obstructions and openings:
if one is gravely ill or lacks the necessary strength,
it will be of no benefit whatsoever to merely cast away one's life.
In accordance with this, there would be no offense; conversely, in all cases contrary to the above, an offense is committed.
Eighth, the explanation of the text:
Among these, there are three:
first, one should practice releasing living beings in accordance with reason;
second, one should rescue others from being killed.
The third discourse concerns saving those who have passed away.
It consists of three parts:
the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion.
The first part, "One who practices the act of releasing living beings with a compassionate mind," is the thesis statement.
The second part, beginning with "All men... and so forth, is the explanation;
it clarifies how one saves living beings.
Regarding the reason for not killing, there are two interpretations:
first, the contemplation of universal kinship; second, the contemplation of equality.
Within the former, it is first clarified that all men and women are one's own parents.
This distinguishes and establishes the true principle.
As for the claim that "killing and eating [the animal] is equivalent to killing one's own parents," this clarifies that such a position violates reason and is therefore untenable.
Question: If that were so, one would incur the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) for killing.
Answer: Because there is an interval between lifetimes, it is not an offense of immediate retribution.
Second, because they also kill me, the lower part of the body clarifies the contemplation of equality.
It means that the bodies of all sentient beings are composed of the four great elements.
Since my own body in the past also once took up these same elements, therefore,
that [other] self and I are identical in our possession of the four great elements.
Therefore, it is said that harming others is to harm one's own body;
this concludes the third point on constant practice.
Second, "If one sees worldly people... and so forth, concerns saving others from being killed.
Furthermore, it is logically necessary to rescue and deliver others through the two aforementioned types of contemplation;
how much more so should one rescue and deliver living beings through the dharma of one's own compassionate mind.
Third, "Constantly Teaching and Transforming" below clarifies that one must first provide salvation through preaching; herein are two parts.
First, a general overview:
preaching the precepts enables people to recognize their transgressions, sever evil, and cultivate goodness, thereby achieving salvation.
Second, a specific analysis concerning those who have passed away.
By expounding on the merit that serves as the perfuming cause, it is shown that the deceased shall behold the Buddha;
this clarifies the benefit accomplished.
Thus far has been clarified the transgression resulting from conduct contrary [to the precepts].
The above has briefly revealed the characteristics of the ten precepts.
The exhortation to practice and study them is as set forth in the "Chapter on the Extinction of Sin," where each point will be explained in detail below.
It is exactly as stated there. 21.
The Precept on Not Repaying Enmity with Lack of Compassion and Patience. Regarding the first intention for the initial establishment of this precept:
it is the principle that a bodhisattva ought to practice patience inwardly while compassion overflows outwardly.
Yet, to instead respond with anger, abuse,
or physical assault is an extreme transgression; therefore,
this rule was established to restrain such behavior.
There are also three [faults] specifically revealed:
resentment does not cease,
and the virtue of patience does not increase.
Sentient beings have all abandoned [the precepts];
since they have thus deviated from the three clusters [of pure precepts], these strict regulations are established.
Regarding the two stages:
previously, seeing suffering, one did not rescue;
now, one gives recompense to the enemy.
This is because it contradicts right practice.
Third, regarding the explanation of the name:
internally lacking compassionate conduct, one externally initiates retaliation against grievances.
The precepts prevent these faults;
therefore, they are so named.
Fourth, regarding the "possession of conditions," it means possessing four conditions.
First, there is the object of resentment;
second, the arising of a mind of anger;
third, the movement of body and speech.
Fourth, it constitutes an offense because it fulfills the ultimate conditions.
Fifth, regarding the deficiency of conditions:
If the first condition is lacking, one commits a grave offense of the first category (pārājika),
because one gives rise to anger and so forth toward an object that is not an enemy.
If the second condition is lacking, one incurs a light preparatory offense (sāmantaka).
Because there is no mind of hatred and other factors are not grave,
the third condition for obtaining a grave preparatory effort (*prayoga*) is missing;
although physical or verbal acts of hatred and so forth do not arise, they are not grave.
Next, the fourth condition is also omitted because it involves repeated preparatory effort (*prayoga*),
as the matter has not yet reached its culmination.
Sixth, regarding gravity and lightness:
The objects of resentment vary in depth;
the arising of anger varies in coarseness or subtlety;
and the preparatory application varies in intensity or mildness.
As for the preceding offenses, how much suffering do they entail?
They are all either light or heavy, intermingled in varying degrees, and each possesses both light and heavy aspects;
one should understand this according to the established rules.
Regarding the seventh point, "perviousity and obstruction": it refers to whether one acts for the purpose of punishment to induce repentance,
or for the purpose of subduing to establish one in virtuous conduct.
If, although one repeatedly applies the antidote, the afflictions are so heavy that they arise unconsciously,
one should be considered not to have committed an offense. Conversely, in all cases contrary to this, one commits an offense.
There are five parts to the explanation of the text:
first, citing the transgression and establishing the formal regulation;
second, explaining how committing it constitutes a violation of conduct.
Third, citing minor matters to illustrate major ones.
Fourth, distinguishing the Path from worldly ways.
Fifth, explaining that intentional transgressions constitute offenses.
At the beginning and middle [of the sequence], there are first two types regarding one's own resentment:
namely, anger refers to mental action (*manas-karman*),
while striking refers to physical action (*kāya-karman*).
Speech arises following two [conditions];
this is stated briefly and not fully enumerated.
If it were to be complete, one should say: "responding to abuse with abuse."
Furthermore, because one who is killed has no immediate retribution to offer,
it is not said that "killing repays killing. If one kills one's parents,
or commits offenses against a sovereign or a parent, the enmity is likewise twofold.
That is to say, with respect to parents, one relies on the sphere of filiality;
with respect to a ruler, one relies on the sphere of loyalty.
According to the principles of filiality and loyalty, one ought to provide a corresponding recompense.
If one repays enmity with enmity,
the cycle of enmity will never come to an end; only by being free from enmity can it be brought to an end.
Only then will resentment cease.
For this reason, the Tathāgata, out of compassionate salvation, established these strict precepts;
hence it is said that one must not seek retribution.
Second, regarding the retribution for killing, the following explains how this violates principle and contradicts proper conduct.
"Life" (*sheng*) refers to the vital breath (*mìng*).
This means that having taken life, one repays it with life.
Therefore, it is said that one "kills. It is not the case that retribution arises from killing; for this would contradict reason.
The phrase "not conforming to filiality" clarifies that such conduct deviates from the Way.
Question: Within the conventions of worldly etiquette, it is said that failing to avenge the enmity of one’s sovereign or father is not filial.
Why, then, would avenging such enmity within this [path] constitute a lack of filial piety?
Answer: The Way is contrary to worldly convention.
The secular world relies solely on the present and does not speak of the causes, effects, and karmic retributions of the future;
yet now, if one were to repeatedly repay their bitter karma,
it would become so abundant as to cause their sovereign and father to sink into eternal kalpas.
How could this constitute the way of filial piety?
Furthermore, why must these enemies necessarily have been one's own parents in a previous life?
If one were to kill them now, how could it ever be considered an act of filial conduct?
Therefore, it is said that this does not accord with the way of filial piety.
Third, "one should not even keep" and so forth clarifies the principle of using a minor case to illustrate a major one:
if one keeps male and female slaves and strikes them physically or reviles them verbally, anger and affliction will arise accordingly.
Among the transgressions of the three karmas, those of speech are particularly prevalent;
hence it is said that verbal offenses are immeasurable.
This statement refers to even minor [offenses], yet they still constitute immeasurable sin.
How much more so, then, given the gravity of the offense; thus it is said, "how much more" (*jue*).
The transgression of the seven reversals (*saptānantarya*) ought logically to entail immeasurable and inescapable retribution.
Furthermore, one who has left the household life (*pravrajita*) distinguishes themselves through the Way, differing from the laity.
Although both laypeople and monastics equally commit this offense therein,
the fault is particularly grave for those who have left the household life; therefore,
it is specifically and emphatically raised so that they may abandon worldly ties and cultivate universal compassion for the sake of all beings.
On the contrary, one repays those very ones with hostility;

this deviation from proper conduct is extreme. Therefore, the fifth [section] is composed below to clarify that violating [the precept] constitutes an offense, as can be understood from the summary of the transgression.
22. The Precept on Contempt for Persons and Disparagement of the Dharma. Regarding the second part of the twenty-second precept, the initial intent of its formulation is as follows:
It is only right that the Bodhisattva should have endured a thousand nails in his body for the sake of the four lines of verse,
and have cast away his life from a high cliff for the sake of half a stanza;
he even offered his royal body as a bed for the rākṣasa.
Using celestial robes as a seat for a jackal,
and honoring ghosts and animals as superior to the exalted rank of the Heavenly Kings—
none of these fail to prioritize the Dharma above all else.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
"For the sake of seeking the Dharma, and because the Dharma is difficult to obtain, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas [exert themselves]."
The one who could bestow the Dharma spoke thus:
"If you can cast yourself into a fire-pit seven fathoms deep,
I shall give you the Dharma."
Upon hearing this, the bodhisattva rejoiced immeasurably and reflected:
"For the sake of the Dharma, I would even undergo immeasurable suffering within the Avīci hell and all other evil realms."
How much more so for one who has entered the human realm and encountered even a minor pit of fire to hear the Dharma!
How marvelous that the True Dharma is so easily obtained,
sparing one from the immeasurable agonies of hell!
"Enter the small fire pit so that you may hear the Dharma.
You simply preach the Dharma;
I shall enter the fire pit."
Such as the Bodhisattva Dharmarājaparyeṣin, the Bodhisattva Vajracintin, and others.
It is further said:
"If someone were to explain even a single phrase of the Dharma for my sake..."
To cause my bodhisattva practice to attain purity,
I shall grasp this great fire filling the trichiliocosm;
from the Brahma-heaven, I shall hold this fire with my body.
They do not consider it difficult;
such being the case,
how much less would they intentionally disparage others or lose the Dharma?
Because the harm is extremely grave,
it must be regulated.
There are also three distinct manifestations.
First, the increase of delusions through negligence;
second, the loss of the Dharma and deviation from goodness;
third, leading others into error and entrapment.
It must be regulated because it destroys the practice of the three aggregates.
Second, regarding the intent [of this regulation]:
whereas previously one would retaliate against an enemy, [here one does not].
Now, one fails to show respect toward those with virtue;
furthermore, having previously increased one's own delusions and karma regarding objects of enmity,
one now loses the benefits of the Dharma due to arrogance toward those who possess virtue.
Third, regarding the explanation of the name:
when one gives rise to pride toward others and abandons the quest for the True Dharma,
the precepts prevent this fault.
Therefore, it is named as such.
Regarding the fourth, the "conditions for completion," there are likewise four conditions for an offense:
first, another who is inferior yet possesses virtue.
Second, giving rise to pride by holding oneself in high regard;
third, conceiving contempt for others;
fourth, abandoning [the practice] and failing to seek the Dharma.
Regarding the five cases of deficient conditions:
the first case lacks the light preparatory effort (*prayoga*);
the remaining three all lack the heavy preparatory effort.
This can be understood according to the preceding explanation.
Sixth, regarding gravity and lightness:
there are degrees of seniority among the virtuous.
Arrogance has its degrees of thickness;
the light-minded heart has its measure of excess;
the relinquishing of the Dharma has its depths and shallows.
As for the sequence and the intermingling [of these factors], there are both light and heavy degrees;
this can be understood by referring to the commentary.
Seventh, regarding "penetration and obstruction":
If one is ill, or lacks strength;
if the other truly lacks virtue yet appears to possess it;
or for the sake of subduing them.
If it is for the sake of taming other sentient beings,
or if their pride and delusions are so fierce that the power of the remedy is weak,
one should likewise not commit an offense.
If one commits a minor offense out of negligence, it is considered grave;
conversely, the opposite cases are all grave.
Regarding the eighth section, the explanation of the text, there are likewise five parts.
First, being naturally ignorant;
second, giving rise to pride based on false conceit;
third, disregarding and abandoning those with virtue.
Fourth, establishing prohibitions and correctly regulating the offenses of transgression.
Regarding the first point, those who have newly left the household life are beginners whose entry into the Path is still shallow.
"One who has not attained understanding" refers to one who has not studied either the Mahāyāna or the Hīnayāna,
and who lacks knowledge regarding every matter concerning the bodhisattva training.
To cite the case of those who have left the household life:
in truth, the same rule applies to those remaining at home as well.
Second, regarding the arrogance arising from false reliance:
One gives rise to ten types of pride based on falsely relying upon ten matters.
First is pride of intelligence (*pratibhāna-māna*),
which refers to relying on one's own cleverness to become distracted, arrogant, and haughty.
Second is the pride of intellectualism (*jñāna-māna*),
which means relying on one's worldly knowledge to disparage the profound Dharma.
Third is the pride of high status (*abhimāna*).
The first is the pride of former office, which means relying on having previously held official rank. The fourth is the pride of seniority,
which means relying on one's advanced age while failing to realize that it is but empty old age.
The pride of the five great castes refers to relying on one's own status as a Kṣatriya or other prominent lineage.
The sixth is the pride of high birth.
This refers to relying on one's own noble ancestry and high status to consider oneself not lowly;
this is the seventh, pride of understanding (*vidyā-māna*). This refers to relying on one's learning.
Worldly dharmas or non-Buddhist texts of the Hīnayāna constitute the eighth pride of merit (*puṇya-māna*),
which refers to relying on one's own past performance of various great meritorious deeds.
9. Pride of Wealth (*dhanamāna*):
This refers to relying on one's own possession of various riches, goods, and so forth.
10. Pride of Treasures (*ratnamāna*).
This refers to the arising of pride by relying on one's own possession of the seven treasures, such as gold and so forth.
Among these ten types of pride, they are subsumed into six prides organized into three pairs:
the first two and the seventh and eighth constitute the pair of merit and wisdom.
The four [offenses] and the ninety [offenses] constitute the pair of body and property;
the remaining three constitute the pair of household and status.
Among these ten, the commission of even one constitutes the conditions for an offense.
It is not necessarily the case that one must commit all ten [offenses] to constitute this;
therefore, the word "or" is used.
The section beginning with "If one does not consult on three matters" clarifies the light abandonment of those with virtue.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a general explanation of relinquishing with lightness;
second, a detailed explanation of the Dharma teacher, beginning with the words "That Dharma teacher... and so forth.

Having recently left the household life, he relied on the aforementioned various forms of pride and failed to consult senior Dharma masters regarding the meanings within the sūtras and vinaya; consequently,
his practice resulted in ignorance in every matter he encountered.
If one exceeds five years [without study], one further incurs the offense of ignorance.
Even among the laity, those who pursue learning may rise to the rank of official;
how much more so for those who have left the secular world, whose primary duty is precisely the pursuit of study?
Throughout three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, you never wasted even a moment;
now that you have given rise to arrogance and abandoned your quest,
how could any practice ever bring accomplishment?
In the second part, the detailed explanation of the Dharma Master, there are also two sections:
first, revealing his lowly status;
second, distinguishing his exalted virtues.
In the preceding section, five matters were briefly enumerated:
first, noble lineage; second, youth.
Third, low status;
fourth, poverty.
These should be understood as the four stages that correspond to the aforementioned ten states.
First, those with incomplete faculties, physically deformed and ugly;
second, those who are actually of low standing but claim to possess high virtue—
whereas those who truly possess virtue have high and superior excellence in both clarity and conduct.
The phrase "all sutras and so forth" clarifies that their wisdom understands what is profound and far-reaching.
Fourth, from "those who have newly begun their training" onwards, it clarifies the establishment of prohibitions and formal regulations.
This means that when observing what is taught, one must not observe [the practitioner's] lineage (*gotra*).
Among the five aforementioned cases, one instance has been cited briefly;
in reality, all five matters cannot be observed.
How much less so when a bodhisattva receives the Dharma from a rākṣasa?
The devas prostrate themselves before the jackal.
How can one judge by lineage?
The fifth [point], "not coming down," clarifies the violation of the rule and the resulting offense.
This refers to a brief citation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
In reality, however, the question applies to both truths.
Furthermore, it explains that when compared to worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*), the Buddha’s teachings are both [the conventional and] the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, it is explained that the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is easy to understand, whereas the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is difficult to comprehend; therefore,
he causes [the interlocutor] to ask.
The remainder of the text may be understood.
23. The Sūtra on the Precepts for Those Newly Seeking Training. Regarding the second and third [sections] of the Sūtra on the Precepts for Those Newly Seeking Training:

the original intent of the initial formulation was that, as a matter of principle, a bodhisattva should enter the various realms of suffering to guide sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon the Great Mind and receive the bodhisattva precepts.
The *Āṭānāṭīya-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states:
"If one transforms a single person, causing them to resolve their mind and receive the bodhisattva precepts,
this is superior to constructing Buddha-stūpas that fill an entire trichiliocosm."
Furthermore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
"For the sake of a single sentient being, one may undergo burning and boiling within the Avīci Hell for immeasurable kalpas,
yet the mind remains as pure as the Most Victorious One."
The commentary states:
If even a Bodhisattva ought to enter the painful hells to transform sentient beings,
how could one allow a beginner to come seeking [instruction] and receive an unfavorable answer?
Furthermore, it increases evil and opposes the wholesome;
one loses the proper occasion and commits an offense. Having thus contravened the three clusters [of precepts], one falls into transgression.
The resulting faults are not minor;
therefore, it must be regulated.
Second, regarding the sequence:
Previously, out of pride, one did not seek the Dharma;
now, out of pride, one does not preach the Dharma.
As the Sūtra says:
The Bodhisattva seeks the Dharma without weariness and expounds the Dharma without parsimony;
this is what is meant by "cloud."
Furthermore, previously one was negligent regarding what had already been learned,
whereas now one regrets it regarding what has subsequently advanced.
As the Sūtra says:
This refers to not disparaging those who have not yet studied, but respecting those who have already studied as if they were Buddhas.
Third, regarding the explanation of the name:
It is called "precept" (*śīla*) because it prevents the fault of failing to guide those who are newly trained and failing to transmit the teachings correctly,
thereby causing the Dharma to perish quickly. Thus, this is its name.
Regarding the four conditions for the presence of causal factors: there are five conditions that constitute an offense.
The first is understanding the Mahāyāna for oneself.
Second, seeking [teachings] from those who are newly trained;
third, relying upon one's own power or status;
fourth, giving rise to thoughts of contempt and the like.
The five types of non-dharmic responses constitute intentional offenses.
As for the five deficiencies of conditions:
If either of the first two [factors] is missing, it is a light preparatory effort (*prayoga*);
if any of the latter three are missing, it is a heavy preparatory effort.
This may be understood according to the commentary.
Regarding the six points of lightness and gravity:
there are varying depths in one's own understanding,
and there are differences in the earnestness or laxity of the seeker.
The degree of one's reliance on power varies;
the arising of thought has its weightiness;
the answers and questions have their right and wrong.
Whether both are light or both are heavy, or whether they are interwoven in varying degrees such that there is both lightness and heaviness,
may be understood according to the commentary.
Seventh, regarding "penetration and obstruction":
If one is ill, or lacks strength,
or does not understand,
or if that person is arrogant regarding the Dharma.
If one acts for the sake of disciplining them,
as previously stated, there is no offense in any case; conversely, in all other instances, there is an offense.
Regarding the eighth section, the explanation of the text,
there are two parts within it.
First, the ritual for receiving the precepts is clarified.
Below, the section beginning with "Furthermore, if the Dharma Master" clarifies the transgressions resulting from violating the practice,
as previously mentioned; within that, there is the chapter on receiving the Bodhisattva precepts,
which has been explained separately.
This text contains three parts:
first, self-vowed reception;
second, reception from a teacher.
Third, the explanation of the intent of one's own vow.
This also has three parts.
First, at the time of initially receiving the precepts.
This means that because there was no formal self-vow to receive [the precepts] while the Buddha was in the world, it is said to be "after his extinction.
"Desiring to" refers to the sincere mind that aspires to and seeks the precepts.
"A good heart" refers to the mind of bodhicitta characterized by pure faith in accordance with the Dharma.
These two are cited because they serve as the vessel for the precepts.
Second, regarding the section "before the Buddha and Bodhisattvas," this clarifies the matter of receiving the precepts.
As for the phrase "before the images of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas":
This refers to manifesting the perception as if [the Buddha] were present.
With resolve arising from within, one establishes a sincere vow;
with a great aspiration binding oneself, one articulates the *karmavācanā* (ritual formula) orally.
One should teach that the manifestation of the signs constitutes the attainment of the precepts.
The ritual text for the *karmavācanā* is as explained elsewhere.
There are three types of signs to be taught.
One expresses this with single-minded resolve:
"If my mind is false and deluded such that I am truly unable to practice the deeds of the bodhisattvas,
may the Buddhas and bodhisattvas not grant me the precepts."
If it is truly to be given,
one knows that the precepts have been obtained because one’s own mind is realized as true;
second, one knows that the precepts have been obtained because a cool breeze arises from all directions.
Third, regarding the explanation of the conditions for obtaining the precepts within seven days:
first, one performs the seven-day rite,
which means entering a pure ritual arena to repent for those offenses that obstruct the precepts.
Regarding the "auspicious signs," these include such things as the Buddha coming to touch one’s head with his hand, as detailed in the sutras.
For those whose obstacles are heavy, even if a year has passed, if they do not obtain the auspicious signs, they shall ultimately not receive the precepts.
The ritual for these confessions is also as explained elsewhere.
Regarding the reception of the precepts, the following clarifies receiving them from a teacher;
therein, it first indicates that auspicious signs are not required.
For these two reasons, they raise an objection:
"Since the precepts one receives are not dual,
for what reason would there be a need or no need for auspicious signs?"
The sub-commentary explains:
"Because this Dharma Master has received it through a lineage of successive teachers from past generations,
and because this precept-dharma has been transmitted down to us in turn, there is no need for auspicious signs."
"I have vowed not to do so.
"If you yourself recite the *karmavācanā*, and you yourself possess no precepts,
from whom would you have obtained them?"
One must receive it from a Buddha or Bodhisattva;
because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are difficult to identify,
one must rely on auspicious signs to manifest [the transmission] before the precepts can be obtained— thus, such signs are required.
Third is the "concluding by means of a subsequent statement," which means that if one receives the precepts with a sincere mind toward the teacher,
the precepts are obtained immediately; therefore, formal ritual gestures are not required.
Third, regarding "if within a thousand li": this explains the intent of one's own vow.
If there is a preceptor within a thousand li, yet one treats them with contempt and does not receive the precepts from them.
Even though one makes a vow, one does not obtain the precepts.
This concludes the explanation on receiving the precepts.
Second, from "If a Dharma Master... onwards, it clarifies the transgressions resulting from violating the practice.
Among these, there are five phrases:
first, relying on one's own understanding;
second, depending on external high status.
Third, newly arrived seekers come to request [instruction].
Fourth, three types of mental states arise within.
Fifth, one provides an answer that is not in accordance with the Dharma.
Therefore, this constitutes an offense.
As for the three mental states:
first, treating the person before one with contempt.
Second, because envy gives rise to resentment, it is called "an evil mind.
Third, arrogance involves looking down upon others.
Since one commits an offense by transgressing against any one of these three conditions, they are so designated.
