Furthermore, one must not listen to music, as clarified below in the precept on listening to music.
Within this, ten types are briefly explained:
the first nine individually distinguish the sounds of the nine kinds of musical instruments,
while the last one collectively concludes the discussion on instrumental music.
This may also be understood.
Third is the precept against engaging in gambling and games of chance.
Within this, there are nine kinds of games.
The third is the game of *pāraseka*,
which is a military exercise from the Western Regions.
It involves two people each holding more than twenty small jade pieces.
Riding elephants or horses,
one contests for the strategic thoroughfare on the board to achieve victory.
As for the four types of *tanqi* (stone-tossing games):
This refers to snapping one's fingers to strike a gaming piece;
winning by making it travel a greater distance constitutes victory.
Regarding the five-word phrase "six-fold gambling" (liù bó), there are two interpretations.
One interpretation states that this refers to the "pair of sixes.
Another interpretation identifies it as six distinct types of gambling games.
The former explanation is taken as definitive.
The sixth and seventh [cases] may be understood as before. Regarding the eighth,
"holding a jar," this refers to holding a staff over a jar, as in the case of Xi Kang and others.
The nine and eight paths of the city of practice can be understood.
Regarding the clarification of demonic arts beneath the "Four Fox Mirrors," five types are briefly distinguished therein. First, as for the "fox mirror":
I have heard that in the Western Regions, practitioners of arts apply medicinal substances to the claws of foxes.
By chanting incantations over it, one immediately perceives matters such as good or bad fortune within its surface;
thus it is called the "fox-mirror.
Second, there is the practice of performing arts using *zhicao* (fungus/herb).
Third, he consecrates the willow twigs with mantras.
Fourth, he consecrates the almsbowl with mantras.
Fifth, he uses human skulls together [with other items] to perform divination and discern good and bad fortune.
All of these are the deeds of the foolish and ignorant;
how could they be appropriate for one engaged in spiritual practice?
Therefore, he strictly prohibited them all.
The fifth is the precept against acting as a messenger for thieves;
this refers to serving as a messenger for thieves to assist them in committing acts of theft.
This is categorized according to its role in facilitating another's commission of theft.
One commits this offense by performing what should not be performed, thereby violating the first of the preceding categories of precepts.
211b: A general summary. 3. If intentionally...
[and so forth], the conclusion regarding the offense can be understood.
34. Upholding the Precepts of Mindfulness. Regarding the intent of the initial formulation of this precept:
it means that the Great Bodhicitta is the root of all practices and the cause for attaining Buddhahood.
If one forgets this mind, then one conceals its myriad virtues;
having already ruined the three clusters and lost the five stages,
what Bodhisattva could there be?
Therefore, it must be regulated.
As for the second point regarding the sequence:
the former regulation was intended to cause the severing of evil.
Now, because this strategy commands the cultivation of virtue,
one first severed the gross evils of body and speech,
and now severs the subtle thoughts within the mind.
Third, regarding the explanation of the names:
it means that even for a single moment of divergent thought, strict regulations are established;
how much more so for other coarse transgressions.
Therefore, the name is established based on what is being guarded against.
Furthermore, it prescribes that one must firmly uphold the precepts and exhorts one to guard the mind.
The name is derived from that which is prescribed.
Regarding the four factors of completeness (*samanvāgama*),
there are three conditions for an offense.
First, one feels revulsion toward one's own arrogant conduct;
second, one takes that fruit as the object of one's school;
third, one abandons this to seek that.
One may commit [an offense] in a single thought-moment.
Regarding the five deficiencies of conditions:
each deficiency constitutes a grave preparatory act.
This can be understood.
Regarding the six grades of lightness and heaviness:
the degree of revulsion toward existence varies in depth.
The conditions [for existence] are manifold;
because the seeking of existence is both temporary and eternal,
there is thus lightness and heaviness.
Know this according to what precedes.
Regarding the seventh point, "penetration and obstruction":
if the power of past habituation momentarily gives rise to a manifest activity.
If they have newly resolved their minds and momentarily lose mindfulness;
or if they manifest in conformity with them;
or if they are disciplining sentient beings.
In all these cases, there is no offense;
in all other instances, there is an offense.
Eighth, regarding the explanation of the text:
The text contains four sections:
first, the regulation for firmly upholding the precepts;
second, the regulation for maintaining great faith.
Third, the restraint of protecting the great resolve;
fourth, the offense of intentional transgression.
Regarding the first [of these], there are two parts.
First, the explanation of the method:
this refers to regulating the four modes of deportment and reciting and upholding the precepts during the six periods of the day and night,
while personally examining one's three karmas to ensure there is not even a speck of transgression.
Regarding the second section on providing analogies:
"Like a diamond" clarifies that the mind is held with such firmness that nothing can destroy it.
Second, regarding "carrying a life-preserving bag," this clarifies the application of a firm mind to correctly uphold the categories of precepts;
whether the offenses are light or grave, not even a hair’s breadth shall be transgressed.
Just as one with a leather air-bag sinks if it leaks even a speck of dust—
details as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*—
thirdly, there is the monk who is like a grass-tie.
According to the *Vyūha-śāstra*,
there were certain bhikṣus who were stripped of their robes by bandits and lay prostrate on the ground, naked.
He bound him with grass, roots and all.
After one night had passed, he could not move.
While hunting, the king saw him there in the grass, naked.
Thinking he was a non-Buddhist,
a bystander replied,
"He is a disciple of the Buddha."
How is this known?
Because his right shoulder was entirely black, which is the mark of one who has bared his upper body.
The king then asked him in verse:
When looked at, he appears to be free of illness;
he is robust and possesses great strength.
How is it that he has been bound by a mere blade of grass?
Day and night he did not turn over on his side.
The bhikṣu answered in verse:
"This grass is extremely fragile."
How could there be any difficulty in cutting [the hair]?
It was only because he had been restrained by the Vajra Precepts of the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
that the King, having conceived faith, released him and gave him his robes.
Upon arriving at the palace, he was provided with new garments and various offerings; therefore,
it is known that by upholding even minor precepts, one does not begrudge even body or life.
If even the Hīnayāna is thus,
how much more so the Mahāyāna?
Second, "always generating" clarifies the observance and maintenance of great faith.
This means believing and knowing that one is oneself a Buddha-to-be who has not yet attained completion;
for it is believed that the Buddha-nature definitely exists and that through practice,
one will certainly achieve realization.
This refers to the certainty of the cause of faith.
The Buddha is one who has already attained realization;
one should have faith that he, too, was once like oneself, practicing and achieving realization as one does now.
This is the fruit of faith.
Because of this faith, one's practice does not regress.
Third, from "arousing the bodhicitta" onwards, it clarifies the regulation and protection of the great mind.
This means that by virtue of the aforementioned faith, one causes the bodhicitta to continue from moment to moment without even a brief moment of separation from the mind; thus it is said.
Fourth, "if it arises" clarifies the violation resulting from contradicting the commitment.
In the "Chapter on Pure Precepts" of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*,
it is stated that even if a bodhisattva should give rise to immeasurable worldly thoughts, this is not called a transgression of the precepts;
however, if they give rise to a single thought of the two vehicles, this is called a violation of the bodhisattva’s pure precepts.
The extensive and the narrow measurements are fully as described therein; they may be understood from that source.
35. The Precept Against Failing to Form Great Vows. Regarding the original intent of this initial regulation:
great vows serve as a transformative cultivation that causes the myriad practices to increase.
Without establishing great vows, there is no way for practice to arise;
therefore, they must be formulated.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
Not to give rise to the great vow is an activity of Māra.
Regarding the sequence of the two [stages]:
first, one prevents the mind from inclining toward the Two Vehicles.
This is because one now vows to seek and pursue the Great Practice.
Third, regarding the explanation of the name:
it is established based on that which is prevented and that which is restrained.
Regarding the four conditions for being fully endowed, there are likewise three conditions:
first, the arousal of a vow without a [discursive] mind;
second, not desiring that which is vowed.
Third, if one has made a vow [not to commit it] but quickly forgets it, one incurs an offense.
Regarding the fifth point, those who lack the necessary conditions all incur offenses of preliminary preparation (*prayoga*), as should be understood.
Regarding the six types of lightness and heaviness:
because one fails to make a vow and thus abandons the practice one has undertaken, there is a degree of much or little;
hence, there is lightness and heaviness.
Furthermore, because there are instances where the original vow is forgotten for a long duration or a short duration,
it can be understood that there are degrees of gravity and lightness.
Seventh, regarding penetration and obstruction:
a bodhisattva at the initial stage of mind must rely upon great vows to bring their great practice to fulfillment;
failing to do so constitutes a transgression.
If one has already attained the stage [of realization], one's former vows have long since been fulfilled;
even if one does not newly generate them, there is logically no transgression.
Eighth, regarding the explanation of the text:
The text contains two sections:
first, the injunction to formulate the great vow;
second, the definition of the offense for violating that injunction.
The preceding section has five parts:
first, establishing vows for filial conduct;
second, aspiring for superior teachers and friends.
Third, may they hear the Great Dharma;
fourth, may they practice according to what has been taught;
fifth, may they maintain their practice with steadfast resolve.
At the beginning and throughout, one should constantly give rise to filial piety; there are three objects toward which one should be filial:
first, one's parents, who possess the kindness of giving birth and raising;
second, the teachers and monks, who possess the kindness of instruction and guidance.
Third, the Three Jewels are fields of merit and sources of grace;
because they are all objects of profound grace, they constitute the sphere of filial piety.
Second, from "Constantly vow" (*chang yuan*) onwards, it clarifies the regulation of vows regarding the cultivation of good teachers and friends.
Within this, there are also three types.
The first is the excellent teacher,
who instructs [the student] in the correct practices cultivated by bodhisattvas.
Second, those who study together: they share the same teacher and the same practice.
Third, virtuous friends and spiritual mentors (*kalyāṇamitra*).
It is not necessarily that they shared the same teacher;
rather, they simply practiced together and supported one another.
Both of these are superior conditions for the accomplishment of practice.
Therefore, I wish to obtain it.
Third, I constantly instruct those below to aspire to hear the Great Dharma;
this refers to why I aspire to [meet] superior persons above.
"I hope you will teach me the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya.
This is the general statement;
"the ten stages of departure" and so forth are the specific statements.
This refers to the path by which a bodhisattva proceeds toward the fruit of Buddhahood; namely,
the stages of the three levels of worthiness and the ten levels of sagehood,
which constitute the essentials of what is to be practiced.
Therefore, I wish to hear the explanation.
Fourth, regarding my aspiration to practice based on that understanding:
this means that once I have attained such understanding, I aspire to practice each and every point exactly as it has been taught.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, after a bodhisattva has sought the Dharma, they reflect:
"One who practices according to the teaching attains the noble Dharma;
it cannot be attained through mere verbal expression alone."
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, among the four types of "approaching" (*upaniṣad*), it is likewise stated that practice constitutes the culmination.
Fifth, regarding "firmly maintaining" and below, this clarifies the firm maintenance of vows and practice;
that is to say, because one firmly maintains the precepts and vows so that they continue uninterruptedly from moment to moment.
2. If one does not cultivate the ten vows below, the nature of the transgression can be understood.
36. The Precept on Not Arising the Ten Vows, the Thirty-sixth. Regarding the original intent of its initial promulgation:
This means that because one might fail to establish great vows to constrain oneself and thus allow one's observance of the precepts to become deficient,
one establishes vows to guard the mind and spur the will,
ensuring that the practice of the precepts is first made pure.
Therefore, it must be regulated.
Second, regarding the sequence:
the former corresponds to the arising of the vow in accordance with [the stages].
This is because one now makes a vow in response to what is non-existent.
Regarding the third point, the explanation of the names is the same as before and may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the four factors of completion: three conditions are the same as before;
the fifth is the deficiency of conditions;
and the sixth, regarding lightness and gravity, may be understood as being the same as before.

Regarding the seven cases of being "unobstructed" (atīta): if one is insane, afflicted by illness, momentarily forgetful, or has attained a [higher] stage, one should logically not be considered to have committed an offense.
Conversely, one commits an offense in the opposite circumstances.
Regarding the eighth section, the explanation of the text,
there are also two parts within it.
First, the establishment of the ten vows.
Regarding the subsequent offense of intentional transgression,
there are also two parts within the preceding section:
first, a general statement clarifying the intent.
This means that only after first having formulated the ten vows is one able to understand and firmly uphold the Buddha’s precepts.
Second, regarding the specific details of making these vows,
there are thirteen types within them.
The first twelve great vows concern protecting one's own precepts;
the final one great vow concerns others attaining Buddhahood.
Within the former, twelve great vows are established regarding the precept against sexual misconduct.
The remaining precepts are all to be modeled after this.
Among them, for the first pair of transgressed precepts, one establishes a vow regarding the fiery pit and the mountain of blades, saying:
"I would rather [sacrifice] this body... and so forth.
Comparing the two, one establishes a vow:
while the fiery pit and the mountain of blades harm but a single body, the charms of women do not; they harm many bodies.
Furthermore, the suffering and harm caused by swords and fire among humans are not severe;
the suffering of the fires and so forth in the evil realms is truly immeasurable.
Moreover, this [human] suffering is but momentary.
They suffer for many eons.
Furthermore, after being burned by the fires of the world, they may be reborn in the heavens;
yet, burned by the fire of broken precepts, they enter the evil realms at the end of their lives.

By comparing these, one should rather enter into fire and other such dangers than violate the precepts; thus, one should look down upon the previous violation of the precept against sexual misconduct and establish a great vow regarding the acceptance of offerings from the faithful and so forth.
That is to say, the first six refer to the four requisites offered through faith and so forth;
the latter five refer to the five exquisite sensory objects and so forth.
Regarding these two, in contrast to the offering of robes through faith, he established the vow of having his body bound with glowing red-hot iron.
These various vows are established for three reasons.
First, as this faithful offering is received by one who possesses pure precepts,
if one were now to violate those precepts, it would constitute receiving [the gift] through theft.
Second, because these various donors have faith in the Buddha’s words, they renounce their wives, children, and provisions to give as meritorious offerings.
To now accept them while violating the prohibitions would be a deception;
it would not only mislead the donors but also bring disgrace upon the Tathāgata.
The merit of even a single hair’s breadth of the Great Compassion of the Three Tathāgatas is shared with the disciples of the Bequeathed Dharma, who thereby obtain the four requisites.
How, then, can one consume the Buddha’s blessings while violating the Buddha’s precepts?
As the Sūtra says:
One who has broken the precepts does not possess even a single drop of water;
ghosts will revile them as great thieves.
Therefore, it is better to endure hot iron and the like than to accept offerings while having broken the precepts.
Third, he made a vow regarding food offered out of faith by likening it to swallowing a red-hot iron ball amidst a fierce fire.
Fourth, he made a vow regarding bedding offered out of faith by likening it to lying upon a bed of glowing red-hot iron.
Fifth, he made a vow regarding medicine offered out of faith by likening it to being pierced by three hundred spears.
Sixth, in the presence of those who have offered faith-based dwellings, he makes a vow to cast his body onto ground of glowing red-hot iron.
Seventh, in the presence of those who have offered faith-based respect, he makes a vow that his body shall be crushed by an iron hammer.
Eighth, in the presence of those who gaze upon beautiful forms, he makes a vow to have his eyes gouged out with glowing red-hot iron.
Ninth, in response to hearing pleasant sounds, he made the vow of a thousand spikes piercing his ears;
this means that as the blades were driven through his entire body, they all reached his ears, hence it is called "piercing the ears throughout the body.
Tenth, in response to smelling various fragrances, he made the vow of a thousand blades slicing his nose.
Eleventh, in the presence of delicious food, he made a vow to cut out his tongue with a thousand blades.
Twelfth, in the presence of a fine army, he made a vow to have his body severed by sharp axes.
Regarding these five sensory objects mentioned above, none constitute a violation of the precepts.
Therefore, he made a solemn vow:
first, that he would always wish for sentient beings to attain Buddhahood before himself;
second, that if he did not give rise to the lower-grade insight, it should be understood as a violation of his vow and a transgression.

37. Thus, regarding the precept on entering dangerous places, the thirty-seventh: The original intent of its establishment is that a bodhisattva’s practice requires the full provision of necessary conditions and resources.
Because difficult circumstances lack the necessary conditions, contradict the teachings, and obstruct the Path,
it is necessary to establish these regulations.
Second, as for the sequence:
Previously, it was explained that the mind guarding the precepts is so firm that one does not avoid fiery embers;
now, it is shown that while preserving the body, even the subtle difficulties on the Path are all avoided.
Third, the explanation of the names:
It is also named according to what it prevents and what it restrains.
Fourth, regarding the conditions for its application:
herein, five types of conduct are prohibited.
First, the dhūta practitioner;
second, the itinerant traveler;
third, the meditation practitioner.
The four-month summer retreat (varṣā) and the fivefold confession ceremony (poṣadha) both require four conditions to be fulfilled.
First, to practice;
second, to recognize this as difficult;
third, not to avoid it from afar.
Fourth, because upon entering therein, one immediately commits an offense.
Fifth, regarding those who lack the necessary conditions:
all incur the preparatory offense.
Understand this accordingly.
Sixth, regarding gravity:
there are varying degrees of depth in difficult situations.
The abandonment of practice varies in degree;
the censure of transgressions varies in severity;
and the resulting consequences vary in gravity.
This can be understood by reflecting accordingly.
Seventh, regarding penetration and obstruction:
if one disciplines one's own mind.
Whether for the sake of taming sentient beings,
or because there is no other place to stay even for a moment,
or because there is no better path.
In principle, one should not commit an offense;
conversely, one commits it by acting contrary to this.
Eighth, regarding the explanation of the text:
The text contains four sections:
first, the establishment of the practices to be cultivated;
second, the enumeration of various difficult points.
Third, prohibiting entry by means of a formal regulation;
fourth, committing an offense by violating that regulation.
Regarding the first [of these], within the five categories of action:
First, a general presentation of the three gates;
second, a detailed explanation of the four matters.
Within the former, there are two parts.
First, the subject matter is indicated.
Regarding "the two seasons for *dhūta* practice," this refers to the two seasons of spring and autumn.
*Dhūta* is translated here as *jǔshuài*, meaning to "rub away" or "eradicate" afflictions (*kleśa*).
Second, regarding those who practice seated meditation during both winter and summer:
since these two seasons are characterized by extreme cold and extreme heat, they do not go out on excursions.
For this reason, one restrains one's conduct and cultivates dhyāna.
Regarding the three types of summer retreat (varṣā):
this refers to sitting out the summer according to the teachings to cultivate the long path.
According to the commentary, there should be four types of wandering and five types of *poṣadha*,
but they are omitted from the text for brevity.
The section beginning with "Commonly used" clarifies the ritual implements employed.
Among these, the three robes constitute three items;
together with the images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as one, there are eighteen.
All of these are essential requisites for the body that serve as vital supports for the path.
Therefore, the rules were established for their possession.
Second, within the detailed explanation of the Bodhisattva’s conduct below:
first, when practicing *dhūta* austerities or traveling, one is permitted to possess eighteen items.
Second, specifically revealing the seasons for *dhūta* practice:
that is to say, during these two seasons—neither cold nor hot—one may enter the mountain forests to increase one's cultivation of the path.
Third, from "if it is the *poṣadha*" onwards, there is a specific explanation of the *poṣadha*.
Poṣadha is translated here as "Pure Abiding" (淨住).
It refers to the recitation of the precepts every half-month.
One examines the three types of action; if there is an offense, one causes it to be confessed, and if there is no offense, one remains silent so that the precepts may be pure.
It is called "living together" (sahavāsa) for this reason.
Among these, "newly initiated learners" refers to those who recite the precepts;
"fortnightly and so forth" refers to the time of the *poṣadha*;
and "reciting the ten grave [offenses] and so forth" refers to the precepts that are to be recited.
This concerns the places for the clear recitation of the Buddhas and so forth;
the ritual for the *poṣadha* of a single person and so forth;
and the respective regulations for wearing, maintaining, and receiving the three robes.
Regarding the four types of *varṣā* (rainy-season retreats) and so forth,
this section provides a detailed explanation of the *varṣā-vāsa* (summer retreat), ensuring that each aspect conforms to the holy teachings.
The practices for winter and summer meditation have been omitted here for brevity.
Third, regarding the ascetic practices (*dhūta*), the various difficult locations are enumerated below;
here, twelve such difficult locations are briefly cited.
The first is the national difficulty of having an evil king.
That king did not believe in the Triple Gem;
thus, the dhūta practitioners were not permitted to enter his realm.
There was a difference in elevation between the two lands.
Third, dense thickets of three kinds of grass;
fourth, black lions that devour humans;
fifth, tigers.
Sixth, the fierce;
seventh, water;
eighth, fire.
The path frequented by the nine winds,
the ten thieves, and the eleven venomous snakes.
Twelfth, this summarizes all difficult cases.
Third, one must not go to a place where the lower restraint is not observed;
fourth, if one intentionally goes to such a place in violation of this rule, the offense incurred is as previously explained.
38. The Precept on Improper Conduct While Seated in the Assembly. Regarding the original intent of this initial regulation:
because it is a departure from worldly custom, seniority based on age is not used to determine rank.
In accordance with the Way, seniority is determined solely by the virtue of one's precepts;
this manifests the supreme model for transcending the world and subdues the pride of "I-am-ness" within the mundane realm.
One must establish [the precepts] because they bring about the practice of the three clusters (tripuṇya-skandha).
Second, regarding the sequence:
Previously, it was intended to avoid external calamities;
now, it is intended to ensure internal conformity with the various ritual protocols.
Third, regarding the explanation of the name:
Furthermore, its name is established by virtue of that which it prevents and that which it restrains.
Fourth, regarding the "possession of conditions":
an offense is constituted through four conditions.
First, being among the assembly;
second, knowing the number of years [of seniority];
third, the skillful means for approaching [the goal].
Fourth, if one has already sat down, it constitutes an offense.
Fifth, regarding the deficiency of conditions:
if the first two conditions are deficient, there is no offense.
If the latter two conditions are lacking, one incurs the offense of transgression through expedient means;
or if one merely walks or stands [in such a manner], it is likewise an offense.
Sixth, regarding the gravity [of the offense]:
The assembly has its great and small;
the seating has its upper and lower;
and time has its long and short—all are equal.
The relative gravity [of offenses] should be understood according to the previous standards.
Regarding the seventh point on "permeability and obstruction": if one is deluded or insane, one may preach the Dharma.
If one suspects another is of greater [seniority], one should then take a seat of lower rank.
If one arrives after the assembly has already taken their seats, and is only three or five years younger than those seated in the fourteenth row, there is no offense;
conversely, in all the aforementioned cases, an offense is incurred.
Eighth, the explanation of the text:
The text contains four sections:
first, a general regulation by citing the Dharma;
second, a definitive determination based on the person.
Third, the refutation of the contrary and the praise of the conforming.
Fourth, the conclusion regarding the offense due to contrariety.
Within the former, the sequence of ordination—prior and posterior—is used to clarify seniority and juniority, just as it is in the case of sitting.
All other cases are likewise.
The Vinaya states:
"Upon seeing a senior elder, one should rise and must not remain seated."
Regarding "seeing a junior seat-mate one should not rise," etc.,
within the second section— determining [the rules] by way of persons without asking—
some explain it as follows:
This would cause the fourfold assembly to sit together in a mixed fashion to distinguish seniority; however,
our current interpretation is not so,
for within the community of bhikṣus, status is distinguished among themselves.
The rest of the assembly was likewise so;
thus, the great and small were clearly distinguished,
and men and women, as well as the ordained and the laity, were not intermingled.
Third, "do not be like" excludes what is incorrect to cause one to distance oneself from it;
"such as my Buddha-dharma" reveals what is correct to cause one to cultivate it.
Fourth, it should be understood that for a bodhisattva to fail to comply with this regulation constitutes an offense. 39.

The Precept on Failing to Preach What Should Be Preached. Regarding the thirty-ninth precept, "Failing to Preach What Should Be Preached," the original intent of its initial formulation was as follows:
The various types of bodhicitta are established through the Dharma to save sentient beings,
so as to enable them to escape all calamities and sufferings in both the present and the future; thus,
they are distinguished into four.
First, to cause the increase of clarity and merit;
second, to bestow the practice of the Dharma;
third, to eliminate calamities and hardships.
Fourth, it is because of the salvation of those who have passed away;
therefore, this regulation was established.
Second, as for the sequence:
The former established the ritual for sitting;
the present establishes the ritual for guidance.
Third, regarding the explanation of the names:
The names may be understood from what they are prescribed for.
There are four factors for each of the four [precepts],
the first being the observation of sentient beings.
Second, knowing of the calamity;
third, lacking a compassionate heart;
fourth, failing to provide guidance—due to these factors, an offense is committed.
Regarding the five cases of lacking conditions:
if the first or the last is lacking, there is no offense;
as for the middle two, the offenses of preparatory effort (*prayoga*) may be understood accordingly.
Sixth, regarding gravity and lightness:
one observes whether the calamity is great or small,
and whether the guidance required is difficult or easy.
One's own dullness or wisdom,
whether they occur together or not, and their relative lightness or heaviness, can be known.
Seventh, regarding the seven points of penetration and obstruction:
If one is personally ignorant and lacks understanding;
if the other party does not accept transformation;
or if there is no teacher available to be invited.
One should remain entirely free from transgressions; conversely, one commits an offense in all cases contrary to this.
Regarding the eighth section, the explanation of the text:
The text consists of four parts:
first, transforming [the people] to cause them to cultivate merit;
second, establishing regulations for the preaching of the Dharma.
Third, to rescue those in distress;
fourth, to establish prohibitions against transgressions.
Regarding the first [of these], one teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to perform six tasks.
First, the construction of monastic dwellings;
second, the building of meditation huts and the like within mountain forests;
third, the establishment of fields and gardens for the Three Jewels.
Fourth, to cause the construction of Buddhist stupas and the like;
fifth, to cause the establishment of places for winter and summer meditation and the like;
sixth, to encourage the undertaking and construction of all sites that serve as centers for guiding all practices.
First, it enables all practitioners to rely upon this to cultivate the path.
Second, it establishes for Bodhisattvas the teaching of the Dharma,
bestowing the Mahāyāna and enabling them to cultivate the Great Practice.
Third, if one is afflicted by illness, one should rescue them from their distress.
Within this, there are five [categories].
First, regarding rescuing those in suffering and difficulty, there are four [subdivisions].
First, when one is ill;
second, when the state is beset by calamities;
third, when bandits arise in various regions.
First, regarding the time for seeking merit on behalf of the deceased:
at all such times, one should recite this sutra and provide vegetarian feasts to seek blessings.
Second, regarding the five types of calamities and misfortunes encountered while traveling or descending [to the underworld] that require rescue: there are five kinds.
First, when one's livelihood is unfavorable;
second, the calamity of fire;
third, the calamity of water.
Fourth, the calamity of wind;
fifth, the sea-rākṣasas.
It is said that when fearing any of these various calamities, one should preach this Mahāyāna.
Third, regarding the section on saving one from the retribution of sins down to the lowest level:
all retributions for sin can only be saved from by the Mahāyāna.
As for these three types of retribution:
First, retribution in the present life;
second, retribution in the next life;
third, retribution in subsequent lives.
This extinguishes the sins resulting from these three retributions.
The seven inversions and eight difficulties may be understood.
Regarding the four types of fetters and shackles, the rescue from the hardships of prison may be understood.
The five [types of beings], such as those with excessive lust, rescue others from the perils of the three poisons and so forth;
in all cases, one should explain that these universally resolve the aforementioned calamities,
all equally employing the Mahāyāna to provide salvation and extraction.
Fourth, regarding the newly ordained, there is the offense incurred for violating the regulations.

The preceding section provides a detailed explanation of the nine precepts; the following section clarifies the summary and exhortation, with the full details to be understood from the extensive texts.
As for the *brahmadanda*, this is translated here as "silent banishment."
It is precisely because those who commit transgressions through irrationality do not submit to discipline that they are governed by this [method].
This meaning is clarified therein.
Therefore, its name may be known. 40.
Receiving Precepts Improperly (Receiving Precepts Non-ritually), Chapter Forty. Regarding the original intent of the initial regulation:
even if sentient beings do not resolve to attain enlightenment, [the precepts must still be conferred].
It is the principle that a Bodhisattva should transform others by causing them to receive the precepts.
How could one allow someone to come from a thousand li away seeking ordination and, with an evil mind, refuse to bestow the precepts?
This would specifically contradict the practice of gathering and nurturing beings, and generally violate the three clusters of pure precepts.
Therefore, it must be regulated.
As for the second point, the sequence:
the preceding discourse on the Dharma serves as the introduction.
This is because it now involves receiving the precepts and gathering the requisites.
Third, regarding the explanation of the name:
it may be understood by referring to that which was established as the rule.
Regarding the four conditions for being fully endowed, there are five conditions:
first, one understands the Sūtras and Vinaya oneself;
second, the other person is free from obstacles or prohibitions.
Third, he comes seeking the precepts;
fourth, this person harbors an evil mind;
fifth, by not receiving [the precepts], one commits an offense.
Regarding the five absences of conditions:
one should understand that the offenses regarding the failure to obtain the means follow in sequence.
Sixth, regarding lightness and gravity:
That is to say: clarity versus obscurity of understanding;
diligence versus indolence in seeking existence;
and the degree of malice in the mind.
The gravity or lightness of [the offenses] regarding whether one has not received the precepts— whether temporarily or permanently, both or neither, and so forth— is to be determined accordingly.
Seventh, as for "penetration and obstruction":
If one has recently recovered from an illness and lacks strength;
or if one is personally dull-witted;
or if the other person does not seek [the teaching] with sincerity.
If a non-Buddhist comes with deceit,
or if one possesses the obstacles and disqualifications [for ordination], there is no offense in any case.
Conversely, all of the above constitute offenses.
Regarding the eighth section, the explanation of the text,
there are five parts within the text.
First, the general inclusion within the vessel of the precepts;
second, instructing on the color of the robes;
third, questioning regarding prohibitions to examine the vessel.
Fourth, one does not bow to the laity due to the four prohibitions.
Fifth, violating requests constitutes an offense.
Regarding the first [of these], there are eighteen groups.
The details are as can be understood from the first explanation of the ten stages mentioned above.
Second, one should instruct them regarding the color of their robes;
herein there are three parts.
Regarding the original regulation for the color of the *kāṣāya*:
*kāṣāya* is translated here as "improper color.
This refers to the five primary colors, such as blue and so forth, which are blended together to produce an improper color; this is termed "deteriorated color" (*rañjita-varṇa*).
Second, from "All dyed garments" downward, it prescribes the colors for other types of robes;
third, from "If in all countries" downward, it clarifies the prescription that these differ from those of the laity—
both may be understood accordingly.
Third, regarding the desire to establish the restrictions for questioning and screening the vessels,
there are also three parts therein.
First, questioning the number to screen the vessels.
Regarding the term "manifesting the body" (*pratyutpanna-kāya*), there are two meanings:
first, it is called "manifest" (*pratyutpanna*) to distinguish it from the past and future;
second, these seven heinous offenses have not yet been lightened through repentance.
The offenses still remain present;
therefore, it is said that one cannot receive the precepts in this lifetime from those who have committed the seven heinous crimes.
However, if one performs repentance in accordance with the teachings, one may obtain them.
Second, regarding the seven heinous offenses (*ānantarya*), the names of those who commit them are listed below;
the meaning of these seven heinous offenses is fully explained in a separate chapter.
Third, regarding all others below, it should be understood that none of them constitute heinous offenses.

4. Regarding the fourth point, "The monastic restrains the body and does not bow to the laity," this means that while the mind maintains reverence, there is no violation of principle. 5. Regarding the fifth point, "Only through understanding...
and so forth, this clarifies the offense incurred by failing to comply with requests.
This refers to those who are not among the seven types of grave offenders but are capable of understanding the teacher's words; yet,
even if such persons come from as far as a hundred *li* to seek ordination,
one might respond with anger and refuse to grant them the precepts.
It is logically appropriate that an offense be incurred.
Regarding the term "evil mind," it refers to [minds] such as those of jealousy for the sake of fame and profit, anger and resentment, or harboring enmity.
Regarding the precepts for all sentient beings, there are two meanings:
first, they are not the precepts given to those sentient beings who seek them;
second, this is merely the name of the precepts.
This means that the Bodhisattva precepts are called "precepts for all sentient beings," because these are the precepts that all sentient beings ought to attain; thus it is said.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
41. The Precept Against Pretending to Be a Teacher While Lacking Virtue. Regarding the first intention for establishing this precept:
there are four cases of one who, without understanding the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, as well as the gravity of transgressions and their observance, acts as a teacher for others.
First, it causes the true Dharma to perish because the transmission is lacking;
second, it causes unrighteous practices to prevail.
Because of erroneous transmission,
there are three ways in which those being transformed are led astray,
thereby preventing others from reaching the state of liberation.
Fourth, one increases one's own evil karma because of greed for fame and profit;
therefore, it must be restrained.
Regarding the second sequence:
previously, when there was truly something to be understood, one refused to give it to those who came seeking it;
now, though truly lacking virtue, one forcibly acts as a teacher for others.
This is because all such things are improper.
Third, regarding the explanation of the name:
it is established to prevent deceptive losses and to ensure that one studies with sincerity.
Therefore, it is given this name.
Regarding the fourth point, the "possession of conditions," it is established by possessing four conditions.
First, the one who is truly without knowledge;
second, those intended for conversion by him;
third, those who crave fame, profit, and the like.
Fourth, one commits an offense immediately upon bestowing the precepts.
Fifth, regarding the deficiency of conditions:
for each deficiency, there is a preparatory offense (*prayoga*).
This can be understood.
Regarding the sixth point, lightness and heaviness:
there are varying degrees of ignorance.
Those to be converted may have sharp or dull faculties;
their greedy minds may be light or heavy;
and the conferral of the precepts may be complete or deficient.
The relative weight of "both together" and "not both together," and so forth, can likewise be understood.
Seventh, regarding "permeation and obstruction":
if one's training is as yet not perfected, [the path remains obstructed].
If he comes to press for [the teaching], one should not bestow it for the sake of profit or other such motives;
otherwise, one incurs an offense. Conversely, if one acts as described above, no offense is committed.
Regarding the eighth section, the explanation of the text,
there are five parts within it.
The first is the discernment of the stage of the teacher’s virtue.
Second, they discipline disciples through mere rules;
third, they actually possess no knowledge;
fourth, they feign understanding for the sake of profit.
Fifth is the formal conferral of precepts and the resulting offenses.
Since, at the outset, one instructs others to give rise to faith and then confers the precepts upon them,
one is thus called a "Dharma Master who imparts instruction."
Second, regarding the desire-realm rebirths, the following clarifies the regulations for instructing disciples.
This section contains four parts:
first, the instruction on requesting the two masters.
This has two meanings. First,
it means that among human beings, one requests these two masters to receive the bodhisattva precepts,
according to the ritual for receiving the ten śrāmaṇera precepts.

Second, one should remotely invite the original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha and others, to serve as preceptors (upādhyāya), and personally invite the preceptor who transmits the precepts to serve as the ācārya. The *Śīla-sūtra* states:
"There are two kinds of teachers."
First is that which is invisible,
namely the Buddha, Bodhisattvas, and the Sangha.
Second is that which is visible.
This refers to the preceptor.
One receives the bodhisattva precepts from these two masters.
Furthermore, regarding the request for five masters as stated in the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra*:
One requests [instruction] from a teacher who is invisible.
When one requests instruction from a single teacher in the *Yogācāra* and other treatises,
it refers exclusively to a teacher who is visible.
The second and third masters should ask; this clarifies that they must inquire regarding the seven impediments (*saptāvaraṇa*).
These seven impediments are precisely the seven reversals (*sapta-viparyaya*);
they are called "impediments" because they obstruct the reception of the precepts.
This sutra asks about seven matters specifically because it is concerned with prohibitions;
however, if one were to rely on both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna meanings,
the *Śīla-sūtra* (Good Precepts Sutra) asks about ten types of matters by way of their virtuous qualities.
Only those who possess [the requisite conditions] may receive the precepts.
Do they possess all three sets of precepts?
That is to say: the five precepts, the ten precepts, and the full set of precepts (upāsaka-śīla, śrāmaṇera-śīla, and upasampanna-śīla).
That sutra concerns the renunciant bodhisattva;
one must possess these three precepts before being able to receive the bodhisattva precepts.
Second, has the bodhicitta been generated?
Third, is he a true bodhisattva?
Fourth, is he able to relinquish all internal and external possessions?
Fifth, is he able to disregard his own body and life?
Sixth, is one able to be without greed regarding objects of greed?
Seventh, is one able to be without anger regarding objects of anger?
Eighth, is one able to be without delusion regarding objects of delusion?
"Ninth, will you not be afraid in situations that inspire fear?
Tenth, are you able to follow all the bodhisattva precepts as I have received them?
To each of these, one should answer, "I am able."
If one were to speak in full detail,
one should first inquire about the seven obstacles and subsequently inquire about the ten superior qualities before one may receive the precepts.
If one is a lay bodhisattva, with the exception of the first [of the ten], all other points are the same as those asked;
there are further questions in the *Susheng jing* (Sutra on Good Birth), which are explained therein.
Third, regarding the instruction below on repenting for the commission of the ten grave offenses (*daśa-ānantarya*).
This refers to the method for teaching repentance to those who have committed the ten grave offenses.
As for the "thousand Buddhas of the three periods," this means that among the Buddhas of the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*, the Tathāgata Padmaprabha was the first.
Down to Viśvabhū Tathāgata— these one thousand Buddhas,
headed by Krakucchanda Tathāgata in the present Bhadrakalpa.
Descending to the one thousand Buddhas beginning with Ruci Tathāgata;
in the future Star-Constellation Eon (*Tārakakalpa*), beginning with Sūryaprabha Tathāgata,
descending to Suvarṇasumera-lakṣaṇa Tathāgata as the final one of the one thousand.
Furthermore, among the auspicious signs seen,
since it does not say "seen in a dream," seeing them while awake is extremely rare.
If one attains these signs,
the original precepts are restored in their entirety;
there is no further need to receive them.
If one does not attain these signs,
the original precepts have already been lost;
therefore, it is said that one does not obtain the precepts in this present life.
Because this constitutes a violation through the highest grade of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*), one loses the precepts;
yet, because they can be received again, it is said that "the precepts are increased.
This "increased reception" refers to receiving them again with greater weight.
Fourth, the confession of minor secondary offenses (*laghu-pāpaka*).
This refers to the method of confession before another person (*pratideśanīya*),
as is the general procedure for a bhikṣu confessing a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Regarding the Dharma treatise on repentance for offenses of these two categories, there are four types:
first, repentance through the Vaipulya Sūtra before the Buddhas of the ten directions for violations of the ten grave precepts committed with intense fetters;
second, repentance before the assembly of the four classes of Bodhisattvas for violations of the ten grave precepts committed with middling or lower fetters.
Regarding the three offenses of the ten grave rules: for the lower grades of the grave offenses, one performs confession before another (pratideśanā) through the preliminary application;
for the four lighter grades of the preliminary application, one performs confession by self-reproach (cittapratyavekṣaṇā).
Within the two grades of light impurities:
The primary offense is confessed before another;
the preparatory acts are expiated through self-reproach,
both as explained in the separate compendiums.
Fifth, the section beginning with "the teacher of instruction and precepts" clarifies that one must thoroughly understand the regulations explained above;
hence it says, "one must understand each point well.
Third, the section beginning with "if one does not understand" clarifies that there is actually nothing known.
Among these, there are five [points].
First, not understanding the dharma of the precepts;
that is, [not knowing] whether [an offense] is light or heavy, what constitutes a transgression and what does not, and what constitutes observance and what does not.
Second, not understanding the dharma of principle,
namely that the ultimate truth is equal and does not contradict the conventional, and so forth.
Third, not understanding the dharma of stages.
That is to say, the stage of the "cultivated seed" (*śikṣā-bīja*) corresponds to the ten stages (*bhūmi*); "nurturing" (*puṣṭi*) corresponds to the ten practices (*caryā*);
and "indestructible" (*asaṃhārya*) corresponds to the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) and the stage of the Vajradhvaja.
The "elements of the path" (mārga-jāti) refer to the ten stages (*bhūmi*),
so called because the noble path (*āryamārga*) remedies the afflictions.
"Correct nature" (*samyaktva*) refers to the stage of Buddhahood.
Because the ultimate fruit is manifested.
Fourth is the lack of understanding regarding the practice of the dharma,
which refers to the extent of the various meditative practices and the boundaries of entering and emerging from meditative absorption throughout the aforementioned stages.
Regarding the ten factors of dhyāna:
these refer to the five factors of the first dhyāna and the one factor of the second dhyāna.
The third dhyāna has four factors,
and the fourth dhyāna has one factor.
Since this sūtra is not the original version, it must be entered into the practice.
"Five hundred and one who did not grasp the meaning" summarizes their ignorance. From "Furthermore, the bodhisattvas...
below, it clarifies those who feign understanding for the sake of profit.
Among these, at the outset, one falsely pretends to understand the Dharma for four reasons:
namely, first, for profit;
second, for fame.
The three types of disciples,
the four kinds of offerings,
and subsequently deceiving oneself and others constitute transgressions subject to censure.
The fifth [point], regarding the clear exposition for those of lower status, and the resulting offense upon its completion, may be understood as before.

42. The Precept on Teaching the *Poṣadha* in an Improper Place. Regarding the forty-second precept on teaching the *poṣadha* in an improper place, the original intent of the initial prohibition was as follows:
The Vinaya is established for the internal community as a secret teaching;
it is not something that non-Buddhists or evil persons ought to hear.
Therefore, it must be regulated.
There are three distinct aspects to this manifestation:
first, the lightness of one's own precepts.
Second, it increases those evil views;
third, it causes others to slander [the Dharma].
For these reasons, it was prohibited.
Regarding the two stages:
the former refers to falsely interpreting for the sake of profit,
while the latter refers to falsely transmitting for the sake of profit.
Third, regarding the explanation of the name:
one should not speak what ought not to be spoken;
the precepts prevent this fault.
Therefore, it is designated by this name.
Regarding the four conditions for its possession, there are likewise four conditions:
first, for the sake of benefit.
Second, in relation to outsiders;
third, the mind is not deluded;
fourth, one commits an offense immediately upon the conclusion of the recitation of the precepts.
Regarding the five deficiencies of conditions:
it should be understood that for each deficiency, one incurs a fault of expedient means (*upāya*).
Sixth, regarding gravity and lightness:
To what extent is there benefit?
There are good and evil among outsiders;
within the mind, there are thoughts and doubts.
In the recitation of the precepts, there are cases where the requirements are complete or deficient; in all such instances, whether they occur together or separately,
the relative gravity of the offense can be discerned.
Regarding the seventh point on penetration and obstruction: if one is facing a king,
or a person of pure faith who practices the path.
If one intends to confer the precepts and first explains them and asks whether the candidate is capable,
there is no offense; to do otherwise constitutes a transgression.
Regarding the eighth section, the explanation of the text,
there are four parts within it.
The first is the general regulation.
Second, the penetration and obstruction;
third, the discernment of wicked persons;
fourth, the violation of regulations and the resulting offense.
Regarding the initial statement that those who have not yet received the bodhisattva precepts are of three types: first,
there are those who do not receive them because they lack pure faith in the bodhisattva path.
Second, although one does not slander, one is still unable to accept [the teaching].
Third, having faith and intending to accept, but not yet having accepted—
these two constitute the completion of the offense.
Second, those who follow external paths cling to their own heterodox ways and seek out faults in the Buddha-dharma;
upon hearing the various minor precepts taught by the Buddha, they would despise and disparage them.
Third, because evil persons, upon hearing the exposition of the Vinaya, would slight and disparage the Sangha, one should not preach it to them.
The mention of "a thousand Buddhas" is used figuratively for a large number.
It means that because all Buddhas alike preach these precepts, they are called the "Great Precepts of the Thousand Buddhas.
This refers not only to the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Second, regarding the section on "Clarifying Permeability and Obstruction" following the discussion of false views:
this precept is intended to restrain those within one's own community;
logically, it is not for them to hear.
It is like a person who does not reveal the location of their treasure store to a thief.
Regarding the statement "except for the king":
the Buddha-dharma was entrusted to two types of persons.
First, a disciple of the Buddha serves as internal protection;
second, a king serves as external protection.
Because these are the persons to whom the Buddha entrusted [the Dharma], speaking to them in this manner constitutes no offense.
Furthermore, since the king possesses power,
he ought to rely upon the Vinaya to exhort practitioners; therefore,
it is necessary for him to know [the precepts].
All others that do not serve this function are completely severed.
Regarding the three [types of] "evil persons," the following explains evil persons.
There are two kinds of evil persons.
First, the stubborn fool.
This refers to one who, though possessing a human body, lacks precepts and is thus called a beast;
for they lack the causes of a human being.
In future lives, they will never again behold the Triple Gem;
like wood or stone, being devoid of mind,
how could they possibly see?
Second, wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
This refers to views that contradict reason, such as regarding wood—which is insentient—as having four [sentient] qualities.
Fourth, it should be understood that for a Bodhisattva, violating the prohibitions constitutes an offense.

43. Therefore, regarding the forty-third precept on violating the prohibitions: the original intent of this regulation was that a bodhisattva ought to protect and uphold the pure precepts even at the cost of their own body and life.
How could one possibly violate one's own fundamental vow without fear of breaking the prohibitions?
Therefore, strict regulation is required.
Furthermore, this precept was established in order to protect all categories of ethical discipline and ensure their firm stability.
Regarding the two sequences:
previously one spoke what should not have been spoken,
whereas now one commits what should not be committed.
Third, regarding the explanation of the names:
they are designated according to what is being prevented.
Fourth, regarding the conditions for their possession: there are likewise four conditions.
First, possessing the precepts within one's own person;
second, facing an object of transgression;
third, intentionally giving rise to the thought [to commit it].
Fourth, one commits an offense through performance.
Fifth, regarding the deficiency of conditions:
this means that for the first and third [cases], there is no offense.
The attainment of the two and four [factors] through skillful means can be understood.
Regarding the six [categories of] light and heavy:
this refers to the strength or weakness of the object.
The mind may involve deliberate deception, and the offenses may be heavy,
light, or equal; these are to be judged according to the preceding principles.
Regarding the seven cases of pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness:

this precept has no separate formulation; rather, if one commits a transgression against any other precept through the mere arising of the intention, one simultaneously commits a transgression against this precept as well.
Therefore, one should understand that both the pervasive and non-pervasive applications are as explained in the sections on the various precepts.
Regarding the eighth section, the explanation of the text,
there are three parts within it.
First, a general mention of the violation of precepts.
Second is the reprimand that exposes the fault;
third is the prohibition that establishes the offense for transgression.
Within the former, the phrase "one who has left home with faith," etc., cites their original vow.
Therefore, the phrase "giving rise to such thoughts" and so forth clarifies the violation of the vow and the resulting offense.
The section beginning with "second, one shall not... clarifies the faults and the subsequent reproach;
therein are eight points.
First, not even a hair’s breadth of the offerings was given;
second, not even a single footstep’s worth of the great earth was taken;
third, not even a single drop of the drinking water was used.
Question: It may be granted that one who breaks the precepts has no share in offerings and gifts;
however, since the water and land of a king are experienced by all sentient beings alike, why does he likewise have no share?
Answer: Laypeople who lack the precepts consume the water and soil of the king and must all pay taxes;
those who have left the household life do not pay taxes, which is truly due to their practice of the precepts.
Now that both of these two types are absent,
how could there be any portion?
To function without a portion— how could that be?
"Is this not a thief?"—
this refers to the four ghosts who block and revile the thief.
It means that if one's observance of the precepts is like a diamond, the deities of the precepts will praise and protect them.
Now that his precepts have been broken and the deity has departed,
five thousand great ghosts will block his path from the front, reviling the thief,
while sweeping from behind to obliterate his way.
Fifth, people of the five generations also revile them,
because they are called thieves who steal the outward forms within the Buddha-dharma and thieves who steal offerings and sustenance.
Sixth, all sentient beings do not wish to see them.
Because they are like enemies who feign intimacy;
seventh, those who violate the precepts and are equal to animals,
because their bodies of sin are identical.
The eighth [offense], "identical to a piece of wood," is so called because there is no cognition. Regarding the three [factors],
one should understand that the destruction of the lower restraint and the destruction of the fetters constitute the offense.
44. Chapter Forty-Four: Disrespecting the Sutras, Vinaya, and Precepts. Regarding the original intent of this initial regulation:
it is because the precepts are the causal provision for the meal that brings about Buddhahood.
That teaching and its principles ought to be respected;
how much more so this Mother of all Buddhas, whom the Tathāgatas themselves revere and honor to the utmost.
How could one possibly place anything before her?

As for the sequence:
previously, he was commanded not to violate the prohibitions and precepts; now, he is regulated and commanded to revere the Dharma.
Third, regarding the explanation of the name:
it is so named because it prevents disrespect toward others and establishes the gravity of the Dharma.
Regarding the four conditions for possession, there are likewise four conditions:

second, lacking a respectful mind.

fourth, committing an offense even without acting;
fifth, the deficiency of conditions.

Regarding the sixth point, lightness and gravity:
there are varying degrees of lightness.
The mind has its lightness and heaviness;
the body has its wealth and poverty;
actions have their goodness and evil.

Seventh, regarding "penetration and obstruction":
if one is ill or impoverished and finds no place to obtain [the requisites], it is obstructed.
Whether one constantly enters deep meditative concentration,
or is intent on saving sentient beings,
or constantly preaches the Dharma.
In principle, there should be no offense; conversely, in all cases contrary to this, an offense is established.
Eighth, regarding the explanation of the text:
The text contains five sections:
first, the regulation for receiving and upholding [the precepts];
second, the regulation for reading and reciting [them].
Third is the scriptural citation.
Within this, the objection is raised first,
namely, that [the body] would be flayed and so forth.
Subsequently, it is easy [to understand] "wood-bark" and so forth; that is to say,
the bark of the *pāṭala* leaf is what is meant by "wood-bark."
The remainder may be understood.
From "the four constants" downwards, it prescribes making offerings, transcribing [the scriptures], and so forth;
