Fifth, it should be understood that if one does not comply with this regulation, an offense is incurred. 45.
The Precept on Not Transforming Sentient Beings. Regarding the forty-fifth precept, "The Precept on Not Transforming Sentient Beings," the original intent of its initial formulation was as follows:
Because the bodhicitta is the cause for attaining buddhahood,
it restrains all bodhisattvas and enables them to transform sentient beings;
therefore, one should cause them all to give rise to this great mind.
The Sūtra says:
"If I were to transform others through the Hīnayāna,
I would fall into stinginess and greed."
This matter is improper;
therefore, it must be regulated.
Second, regarding the sequence:
Formerly, there was a lack of respect for the Dharma;
now, there is a failure to transform living beings.
For this reason, both are prohibited.
Third, regarding the explanation of the name:
abandoning the transformation of sentient beings violates and harms great compassion;
this precept guards against such a fault.
Therefore, it is named as such.
Regarding the four conditions for its possession, there are likewise four conditions:
first, with respect to sentient beings.
Second, failing to give rise to compassion;
third, failing to give rise to skillful means;
and fourth, abandoning them without exhorting or guiding—due to these, one incurs an offense.
Regarding the five deficiencies of conditions:
each deficiency can be understood through its respective application.
Regarding the sixth, lightness and gravity:
Sentient beings encounter difficulties and ease;
their compassionate hearts possess varying degrees of depth;
and their skillful means differ in their extent.
There is no exhortation regarding the temporary or the ultimate;
furthermore, cases where both occur and so forth are to be understood according to the preceding [analysis]. Seventh, as for "penetration and obstruction":
If one is ill, lacks strength,
has not yet attained understanding, or if the other person is difficult to transform,
it is in accordance with principle that there is no offense.
Conversely, all the above cases constitute offenses.
Regarding the eighth section, the explanation of the text, there are four parts.
The first concerns the regulation and transformation of human beings.
Among these, great compassion is the mind that performs the transformation;
the cities and so forth are the places of transformation;
and all sentient beings are those who are transformed.
Proclaiming [the teachings] and so forth are skillful means for transformation;
receiving the three refuges and so forth are the benefits obtained through such transformation.
This has two meanings.
First, regarding the reception of the precepts: first one receives the three refuges, and afterwards the characteristics of the ten precepts are explained.
Second, there are two ways of receiving the precepts:
first, receiving the bodhisattva’s three-refuge precepts.
Second, receiving the ten precepts. Second,
if one observes that those of lower capacities are transformed by the teachings for animals—
meaning they lack the capacity for understanding— one uses these words to awaken them so that they may achieve self-cultivation through habitual perfuming.
Thus, it serves as a remote, superior cause for that [attainment].
For example, in the past, there was a cow that ate grass before a stūpa; upon lifting its head and seeing the stūpa, it subsequently attained liberation.
Third, the Bodhisattva establishes the fixed stage (*vyavasthāna*) below.
This means that one must transform sentient beings and cause them to resolve upon the Great Mind (bodhicitta) before one is truly a bodhisattva; thus it is said.
Fourth, if one does not [act accordingly], the offense is established in violation of the regulations, as can be understood.
46. The Precept on Improper Conduct in Preaching the Dharma. Regarding the initial intent behind the establishment of this precept:
This precept was established so that others might revere the Dharma and increase their roots of goodness,
while one’s own reverence for the Dharma remains in accord with the instructions of the teachings;
thus, it is ordained to accomplish these two benefits and to conform to those three aggregates of merit.
Regarding the two stages:
in the former, one was taught to resolve the mind toward enlightenment; now, one is taught to revere the Dharma.
Third, regarding the explanation of the name:
this name is established based on that which is prevented and that which is restrained.
Fourth, regarding the possession of conditions: there are four conditions.
First, regarding others;
second, dwelling in improper conduct;
third, failing to give rise to compassion.
Fourth, it constitutes an offense because of speaking words.
Fifth, regarding the deficiency of conditions: it should be understood that the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) applies when each respective condition is deficient.
Regarding the six degrees of gravity:
there are those with whom one may speak and those with whom one may not;
there are those who abide in improper conduct, and these vary in depth.
Compassion may be either temporary or permanent;
speech may be accompanied by the necessary instruments or lack them.
Both cases, as well as their equivalents, should be understood according to the preceding analysis.
Regarding the seventh point on penetration and obstruction:
if another’s illness is grave,
or if the power of a king is absolute.
There is no offense. Conversely, all instances contrary to this constitute an offense.
Eighth, regarding the explanation of the text:
The text contains three sections:
first, the prohibition of improper conduct;
second, the instruction on correct rules.
Third is the offense of violating the precepts.
Within the preceding [section], compassion is taught as that which should be constantly aroused because it is the cause for transforming sentient beings;
since those of noble status often harbor arrogance, this is specifically singled out.
There are three types of improper conduct:
sitting while another stands;
and being with two persons who are higher [in status] while one is lower.
While three people are seated, one is not;
among these, the high seat corresponds to the latter two cases.
This can be understood accordingly.
Second, regarding the section "If one preaches the Dharma," this clarifies the correct principles of the teaching;
herein, there are five matters.
First, place the Dharma Master upon a high seat;
second, provide him with offerings of incense and flowers;
third, let those who listen sit on lower seats.
One should revere them as one does one's parents.
One should receive their instructions as a fire-worshipping brahmin serves his sacrificial fires.
As the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states:
If a person’s moral conduct and footing are weak and inferior,
yet they are able to preach the Dharma so that many people enter [the path],
one should provide offerings to them as one would to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and receive what they teach.
Therefore, they are similar.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
"There is one who knows the Dharma."
Whether old or young, all should be venerated as one would a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fire.
Third, regarding the speaker of the Dharma, the following clarifies the transgressions resulting from violating the regulations;
there are three such types.
First is physical conduct, such as standing and so forth;
second is mental intention, such as seeking fame and profit;
third is vocal activity, such as teaching what is not Dharma as Dharma, teaching Dharma as not Dharma, and using worldly speech.

Furthermore, in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, it is stated that only the teaching of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and the teaching of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-dharma*) constitutes the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*);
all others are not. 47.
The Prohibition Against Establishing Rules That Are Not in Accordance with the Dharma (The Forty-Seventh). Regarding the original intent of this initial prohibition:
It is the proper principle for a bodhisattva to protect the Three Jewels even at the cost of one's own body and life;
yet, on the contrary, such a person relies on their power to destroy the True Dharma.
Therefore, it is necessary to establish this regulation.
Regarding the two stages:
previously he preached the Dharma through unconventional means;
now he maintains his majestic bearing to extinguish the Dharma.
Since the transgression is grave,
it is regulated next. Third,
regarding the explanation of the name:
The term "gate" (*mukha*) is used here because it refers to that which is guarded against.
Regarding the four conditions for the four types of upholding, there are likewise four conditions:
first, receiving the precepts with faith.
Second, relying on one's own high status and authority;
third, establishing regulations contrary to the Dharma;
and fourth, causing the destruction of the Buddha-dharma—due to these, an offense is committed.
Regarding the five deficiencies of conditions:
if the first condition is deficient, one incurs a grave offense (sthūlātyaya) but it is not a transgression of the precepts;
if the subsequent condition is deficient, one incurs a grave preparatory offense (prayoga).
The omission of the latter two conditions can both be understood through their application (*upāya*).
Regarding the sixth point, lightness and gravity:
when one relies on authority to establish regulations that subvert the Dharma, there are varying degrees of severity; these should all be assessed according to the same principle.
Seventh, regarding the points of penetration and obstruction:
if one restrains evil persons from leaving the household life or prohibits them from making or selling images,
it is logically not a transgression.
All others constitute offenses.
Regarding the eighth section, the explanation of the text,
there are three parts within the text.
First, a general explanation of the nature of cessation;
second, a specific manifestation of the characteristics of cessation;
third, the intentional commission of an offense.
In the former case as well, there are three types:
first, receiving the precepts with a mind of faith;
second, relying on one's own high status and authority.
Third, it destroys the Buddha-dharma.
Second, to clarify the specific manifestations of the intermediate [state], first:
it obstructs one's renunciation and the cultivation of the Path.
The two obstacles consist of creating images and creating scriptures;
these destroy the sustenance of the Triple Gem,
upon which sentient beings of the period of the Bequeathed Dharma rely for their support.
Now that it has been diminished,
because its transgression is grave,
it is summarized as "the sin of destroying the Triple Gem."
Third, it should be understood that intentionally acting contrary to the teaching below constitutes an offense.
48. The Precept Against Self-Subverting One’s Inner Dharma, the Forty-Eighth. Regarding the intent behind the first formulation:
It is the proper principle for a bodhisattva to protect and uphold the true Dharma, first proclaiming and manifesting it so that it may endure for a long time, thereby repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
How could one permit oneself to destroy the internal community for the sake of profit, thereby harming one's own true Dharma?
Since the loss [incurred] is so great,
it is necessary to establish a regulation.
Second, regarding the sequence:
Formerly they relied on their own majesty;
now they rely on the power of others.
In both cases, they cause harm to the Dharma.
Therefore, they are subject to the same regulations.
Third, regarding the explanation of the names:
that which is prevented serves as the designation.
Regarding the four conditions for the possession [of offenses], there are likewise four conditions:
first, for the sake of fame and profit;
second, reciting the precepts in the presence of a king.
Third, creating obstacles;
fourth, binding those within the assembly.
Therefore, these constitute an offense.
Regarding the five deficiencies of conditions:
for each of the four conditions, there are four types of deficiencies, which may be understood through their respective skillful means.
Regarding the six degrees of gravity:
Regarding the four conditions, one should apply this principle accordingly to determine whether they are numerous or few, and whether they are simultaneous or non-simultaneous.
As for the seventh point, "penetration and obstruction":
if one restrains wicked bhikṣus and the like so that they do not harm the Dharma, [it is unobstructed].
In principle, one should not commit them;
otherwise, all constitute offenses.
Regarding the eighth section, the commentary on the text, there are five parts.
1. To raise up faults so as to cause separation from them;
2. To raise up virtues so as to regulate and cultivate them;
3. To hear of what is improper and thereby encourage self-reproach.
Fourth, how much more so when one acts upon it oneself.
Fifth, intentional commission constitutes an offense.
Regarding the former, first we cite the case of one who originally left home with a virtuous intention.
Next, for the sake of fame and profit, one preaches the fetters of the precepts before kings and others;
this is illustrated by the metaphor of eating what is inferior.
As stated in the *Padmavaktra-sūtra*:
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"For example, when a lion dies, whether on land, in water, or on dry ground, no sentient beings will eat the flesh of that lion's body."
"Only when the lion itself gives rise to worms that eat the lion's own flesh does it perish.
Ānanda, my Buddha-dharma cannot be destroyed by others;
rather, it is the evil bhikṣus within my own teaching who will destroy the Buddha-dharma accumulated through my diligent practice and hardships over three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
The commentary explains:
because those outside the Buddha-dharma cannot destroy it, it is called "not of the non-Buddhists" (*abāhyaka*) and so forth.
Second, regarding the section on "if one receives the Buddha-precepts" and below, which illustrates the cultivation governed by virtue:
One should establish a vow to protect the precepts with utmost sincerity,
like a compassionate mother mindful of her only child,
or like a filial son serving his parents.
There was never a moment when he forgot any of this.
Third, regarding the passage below on "hearing," it clarifies that hearing is not an exhortation to lament.
Within this, he first laments the suffering shared with those in the present.
It can be understood that it would be better to descend oneself and enter the evil realms;
this is all the more so when one commits such acts oneself against those who are dear.
The causes and conditions for both performing [the act] and causing its destruction are as follows:
one who lacks a heart of filial obedience is the cause for destroying the Dharma.
Fifth, if it was intentional, the subsequent clarification of the offense through deliberate action may be understood accordingly.
The preceding section concludes the detailed analysis of the nine precepts.
Second, following these nine precepts, the concluding summary and exhortation to study may be understood.
The preceding section concludes the individual exposition of the minor precepts.
The second section, "All Buddha-sons," concludes [the preceding].
This is recited identically by those of the three periods.
Thus ends the detailed explanation of the two categories of precepts regarding light and heavy offenses.
Third, "All you sons of the Buddha, listen attentively," which concludes by exhorting study.
This section contains four parts.
First, citing the Buddhas' collective recitation.

This means that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time, as well as I, Śākyamuni, have all recited this together, both while on the path of cause and upon reaching the fruit of fruition;
thus one should know that it is essential and supreme.
Second, "You all... and so forth, which exhorts the assembly to uphold it.
This refers to briefly exhorting those assemblies to perform five tasks.
First is "receiving and upholding" (*udgrahaṇa-dhāraṇa*): "receiving" means to accept [the teaching], and "upholding" means not forgetting it.
Second, reading;
third, reciting;
fourth, explaining.
Fifth, regarding transcription:
the three Buddha-natures clarify that the transmission shall never cease;
this means that because Buddha-nature is eternally abiding, the principle of the Dharma is profound and serene.
The *Śīlaskandha-parivarta* and other texts clarify the transmission of the teachings.
Furthermore, it is explained that Buddha-nature is the inherently existing cause for attaining Buddhahood.
The precept scrolls serve as external conditions for transmission;
"transmission" refers to the passing down from the past to the present.
From the present to the future,
because they are transmitted to one another in succession, it is said that they are "uninterrupted.
Fourth, the passage beginning with "attaining vision" clarifies the benefits of the transmission.
This refers to three benefits therein.
First is the benefit of seeing the Buddhas:
that is, obtaining the vision of the thousand Buddhas of this Bhadrakalpa transmitting the succession to one another.
Second is the benefit of being forever separated from evil states;
third is the benefit of attaining birth in a good state,
namely, being born among humans with a body that serves as a vessel for the Path.
This is the section on gathering in sentient beings.
What precedes this concludes the main body of the teaching.
Third, from "I now" onwards is the section on the conclusion and exhortation for circulation.
Among these, four points have been briefly explained in the section on the conclusion;
second, from "You all... onwards, there is the exhortation to study and practice.
Third, "like the signless" (*animitta*) and below refers to that extensive text.
Fourth, "the three thousand" and below clarifies that the assembly hears and upholds it;
this refers to what is explained in detail, one by one, within that chapter.
This caused those three thousand followers to hear it and give rise to joy.
Furthermore, the commentary explains that those three thousand members of the assembly heard the Buddha recite this abbreviated version.
Having given rise to joy, I shall uphold [this teaching].
The explanation of the text being complete,
I express my sentiments in verse:
The extensive version of the Vinaya Piṭaka cannot be seen due to my meager merit;
I long for those bodhisattva precepts.
Exhausting all ignorance through this explanation,
may this maṇi-lamp shine eternally throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Guiding all sentient beings to the place of Great Bodhi.
